speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this day is the day set apart for celebration as the birthday of Her Gracious Majesty Queen Elizabeth II. Last October 14 was the Queen's day, but this is the day on which Canadians have an opportunity of reaffirming their affection and loyalty to Her Majesty.
The Governor General, on behalf of the people of Canada, has sent a message to Her Majesty which reads as follows:
With my humble duty I send to Your Majesty on the day on which we in Canada are proud and happy to celebrate Your Majesty's birthday the loyal and devoted good wishes of your Canadian subjects.
As a reaffirmation and redeclaration of the loyalty of Her Majesty's members of the House of Commons I join with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), and with your leave, Mr. Speaker, in suggesting that we do now stand and sing "God Save the Queen".
Whereupon the members of the house rose and sang

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I was comparing percentages on a certain scale of values for agricultural products sold in 1950 as between western and eastern farms. I said that farmers whose sales amounted to $250 or less were distributed as follows: 72.1 per cent in Newfoundland; 15 per cent in Prince Edward Island; 43 per cent in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; 21 per cent in Quebec; 12 per cent in Ontario and 7.8 per cent in the prairies.
It is sad to note, Mr. Speaker, that on 238,329 commercial farms in our six eastern provinces, 121,329 (about 51 per cent) had sold agricultural products valued at $2,500 or less. Out of this number, 41,896 farms, that is 16 per cent, had made sales amounting to between $250 and $1,200.
If we consider the net income by individual farms in the various provinces, we note that in Prince Edward Island, that income was estimated at $1,586; in Nova Scotia, $963; in New Brunswick, $1,217; in Quebec, $2,195; in Ontario, $3,074; and in the prairie provinces, at $3,227.
If we carry our analysis a little further, we note that the per capita production on the farm was estimated in 1953 at $162 in Quebec, at $304.60 in Ontario, and at $507.60 in the prairies. Such is the situation of our eastern farmers. And I am not the one who compiled these figures. They are taken from the report of the Gordon commission which enquired on the economic and agricultural prospects of Canada. In quoting them, I have no intention of arousing feelings of animosity between western and eastern farmers.
I merely want to show the government, the Conservative members as well as those of the C.C.F. party, that there is not only the wheat problem in our country but also the problem of the eastern farmers whose income is low, whether they live in northern Ontario or in the maritime provinces. They have to find sources of income outside of agriculture to support their family. Many of them work in factories, others work in the bush during the off-season. I may add that many of them
The Address-Mr. Boulanger in the province of Quebec work for the highway department if they are supporters of the Union Nationale, or are favoured in some other way.
It can be said that the eastern farmer works about twelve hours a day, the whole year round. Having lived on a farm in the west for over a year, I know that the western farmer also puts in a long day's work during the period from sowing to harvest time. I also know that many of them, during the offseason spend the winter in the south of the United States and others seek a well-deserved rest in town. Our eastern farmers do not have time to rest; they have not the time to take a vacation because most of our farmers and our settlers, as I said, spend that period in the bush, away from their family, working hard nearly all winter to come back with a few hundred dollars in the spring.
I am sure my political opponents will blame the Liberal party for this situation. It is always easy to clear oneself of blame when one does not want to assume one's own responsibilities, and that has been the case of the Conservative party for the past year. Yet in 1956, the same men, during the provincial election campaign, went about our farm districts claiming that the farmers of the province of Quebec were the most prosperous in Canada.
It should be recognized that the Liberal party has done a great deal to improve the farm situation in our country during the past 22 years, but that government also realized that there was still much to be done. That is why in 1955 it asked an inquiry into the progress achieved and on the prospects of our agricultural economy. At the same time, the Senate inquired into the use of our farm lands. The purpose of those undertakings was to cast light on the whole situation and allow our leaders to draw up a long term agricultural policy.
One other thing that struck me in this report was the scope to be assumed by the demand for farm products in the course of the next 25 years, following the increase in urban population.
Let me quote a few figures based on the years 1951-55. Taking 100 as an index, we see that the demand for the following agricultural products will increase as follows between 1965 and 1980:
	1965	1980
Red meat	
140	218Poultry products 	
136	214Eggs 	
143	231Dairy products 	
129	168Grain 	
122	140Fruit	
138	237Vegetables 	
134	193
The Address-Mr. Boulanger
How will the country satisfy this demand? The Gordon Commission report states that the total area under farming in Canada will increase by close to 2 million acres between now and 1980, which will make the total cultivated area 176 million acres. The report indicates moreover that it is not on that that we must rely to satisfy our needs. It is recognized that we should rather increase the yield by soil improvement, which means that we should increase the yield per acre, per unit of pasture and head of cattle rather than the yield per man-hour.
To achieve this result in the eastern provinces we must look to the improvement of farming methods and to a greater use of chemical fertilizer, especially on pasture land.
In the eastern part of this country we have a large area with a high productivity potential. But these lands must be properly drained and cleared of stones and treated with adequate quantities of chemical fertilizer in order to be profitable. No doubt there will always remain some submarginal farms. In this connection I will offer a few suggestions at the end of my remarks.
For the moment I wish to call the government's attention to the value of family farming to the general economy of this country. I could do no better here than quote the president of the American Farmers' Federation, who stated:
We must neglect nothing that will help to preserve the family character of agriculture, not only because this is a social safeguard in a democracy, but because the family farm unit is the most efficient agricultural production unit yet devised.
Mr. Speaker, having offered these general remarks, I would now like to offer some recommendations whose implementation I would like to see and which would be of great benefit to eastern farmers.
The first recommendation is drawn from the Gordon report. It consists in carrying out a program of geological surveys in the eastern and Atlantic provinces. Part of the mapping work in these areas has already been carried out, but we should nevertheless continue along these lines and speed up the work, while giving priority to those eastern areas which have not as yet been explored.
According to the report there is yet another project of national scope which could be carried out, and that is the classification of lands according to their possible uses, and the regrouping of small properties wherever it is possible. In some cases tree farming

could be carried out more advantageously than agriculture. This classification of soils could be carried out in conjunction with a farm assistance plan in order to help those farmers who would prefer leaving the land to carry out another type of work. In order to bring this plan to a successful conclusion, we will need the sincere and continuous cooperation of the provincial governments and of all interested parties. This plan should be implemented gradually and we should not look for extraordinary results before a certain number of years.
A second suggestion I wish to make to the government has to do with the establishment of an intermediate term and easier credit to allow our farmers, and especially our young people, to carry out a plan of production and systematic operation of their farm.
I would also recommend the granting of a $4 an hour premium on the use of bulldozers by farmers for draining and stone clearing. There are very productive lands in eastern Canada which need only draining and others just as good which need some levelling and stone clearing. It may be something new for some hon. members to hear about stone clearing on farms. This is just to show that conditions in our eastern provinces are very different from those prevailing on the prairies.
Another suggestion which deserves government attention concerns the advisability of better acquainting our farmers with the use of chemical fertilizers. Our farming experts and our experimental farms are doing a wonderful job in that field, but they do not reach the bulk of our farm population. Canada is one of the countries of the world where fertilizers are least in use. We use an average of 3.1 pounds of fertilizers per acre while Australia uses 25.7 pounds, New Zealand 13.8 pounds, the United States 11.6 pounds. I could add that The Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and Japan use more than 100 pounds. I repeat that Canada uses only 3.1 pounds.
With proper use of fertilizers, production could be doubled on most of our farms. Research work done on experimental farms has shown that $1 worth of fertilizer used on pasture lands could bring from $3 to $5 in milk production. It would surely be wiser to spend $5 or $6 million to encourage the purchase of fertilizers than to sacrifice hundreds of millions for the construction of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river to reclaim 455,000 acres of land.

We spend hundreds of millions of dollars every year to support agricultural prices because our lands do not bring enough revenue to our farmers. Let us increase our production to meet our future needs by the use of fertilizers and the problem will be solved while our farmers will get a higher revenue.
These are, Mr. Speaker, a few suggestions which the Liberal party sees fit to bring to the attention of the government in order to save our agriculture and particularly that of eastern Canada.
May I also make a few remarks on the textile industry, particularly that of the province of Quebec. Last year I made numerous representations to the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have even supported the requests of some municipalities of my riding that were seeking help from the government. I would like to read here a letter which a few of my colleagues in this house and myself have written to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), in which we urged the government to help our textile industry. Let me read the last paragraphs of that request.
(Text):
Be it resolved to ask the Minister of Finance to act at once to prevent
1.	The importation of textiles from countries whose standards of living results in lower production costs, and
2.	The importation of goods from those signatories of GATT whose exporters are not adhering to the letter and spirit of this agreement.
(Translation):
We received a reply from the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and I am going to read its final paragraph. The minister said in his letter:
(Text):
For my better understanding of precisely what it is you ask me to do, may I ask you and your colleagues:
1.	Precisely what are the steps that you ask me to take to prevent the importations?
2.	What are the "countries whose standards of living result in lower production costs"?
3.	What are "those signatories of GATT whose exporters are not adhering to the letter and spirit of this agreement"?
4.	In the case of these signatories, what are the goods of which you ask me to prevent the importation"?
(Translation):
Such was the reply we received from the Minister of Finance.
Recently I received from the town of St. Simon, in Drummond county, a resolution asking, among other things:
The Address-Mr. Boulanger
That the city council urge the federal government to revise the tariffs now applying to the textile industry and make necessary and urgently needed amendments thereto.
I forwarded that request to the minister with my comments. Just like last year, the minister asked me: "What do you want me to do?" To which I answered with the recommendations that I am now going to read quickly. They are somewhat similar to those made last week by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard). Here they are:
1.	General increase in the tariifs in order to regain for our industry about 80 per cent of its market;
2.	A revision of the Customs and Tariff act in order to make it more flexible, more adaptable to changing conditions;
3.	Tighter control and supervision by our customs officers;
4.	Better appraisal of imported commodities in order to establish a reasonable production cost abroad and to avoid dumping;
5.	A government sponsored campaign encouraging Canadian consumers to buy Canadian goods first, and Canadian producers to better identify their products;
6.	Temporary reduction of the excise tax in order to give a renewed impetus to the textile industry.
7.	Long term solution: Establish import "quotas" and enforce a practical system of classification and identification of imported goods.
These are suggestions that can be studied and enforced. I believe that with some good will a solution could be found.
A year ago, the government and its supporters charged the Liberal party with being at the source of our troubles in the textile industry. I have here figures from the Cotton Institute of Canada which show that since the Conservative government has been in power, the situation has been deteriorating appreciably in the textile industry. I am just going to read you a few figures. I see that in the third quarter of 1956, we had 22,500 people employed in the cotton industry. During the same quarter of 1957, only 20,800 were so employed, which represents a decrease of 1,700 employees.
Take the fourth quarter of 1956: we had 22,400 employees, and during the last quarter of last year, when the Conservatives were in power, there were 19,800 employees, that is a decrease of 2,600 employees. Nevertheless, we heard during the last electoral campaign that the Conservative government was going to save the textile industry. Furthermore, if we had today's figures, we would probably see that the number of workers is 3,000 less, as compared to the figures of 1956, when the Liberals were in

The Address-Mr. Boulanger power. I am going to quote a few remarks made by this organization. It is said, in connection with imports for example, that the United States have supplied us with 219 million yards of textiles, i.e. 16 million more than the previous year. Imports from the United Kingdom remained at 10 million yards for each year but those from the other countries amounted to 63 million yards as compared to 56 million in the preceding year.
That is the policy of the Conservative government! Once more, it is proposed to settle the textile problem by nice words, but I say that it is not by words that the textile problem will be solved, but by deeds.
I could quote an article published in the Tribune of May 7, 1958. It says in part as follows:
Women's nylon stockings of foreign make sold in Sherbrooke under Canadian label will be exhibited in the Canadian Parliament by Mr. Maurice Allard during the next session. The new M.P. for Sherbrooke in the House of Commons proposes to use these items to prove the unfair competition of foreign manufacturers on the Canadian market.
And there is a photographic reproduction of a pair of stockings sold in Sherbrooke under the label Made in Canada, whereas another label showed their origin as England. Was the hon. representative for Sherbrooke not aware that last year, in 1957, the government had sent a delegation to England with a view to buying from that country? The hon. member was to report to this house with regard to such unfair imports, but he did not do so. For my part, that it is not by means of publicity in press, nor by well-turned phrases that the textile situation will be solved, but by deed and action.
If the hon. member for Sherbrooke is sincere, let him move a resolution. We shall consider it and take a vote.
Back home, in the Drummond riding especially, workers are jobless, and day after day the number of unemployed increases.
Therefore I shall take the liberty, on another occasion, of dealing again with this matter of textiles.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks I wanted to make on the floor of the house. I am convinced that if we get to work in a constructive frame of mind, we shall succeed in achieving progress.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire

in the first place to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure you can understand, by reason of the fact that I entered this house for the first time only last November, that I have personal interest in the contributions made by these two hon. members. The excellence of their presentation and the quality of the substance of their addresses augur well, I know, for their success in this house.
To you, Your Honour, I offer my felicitations. To have been selected as the first commoner during the last session of parliament was a manifestation of the belief that you had the requisite qualities for the speakership, and to be elected a second time is certainly a manifestation of the conviction that you have wise judgment, impartiality, grace and indeed a sense of humour, and I offer my felicitations to the house for having so elected you.
I am very happy, Mr. Speaker, to have this opportunity to report to the house on the deliberations of the ministerial conference which was held under the auspices of NATO in Copenhagen from May 5 to May 7. That meeting was, I am convinced, a successful one. It was not intended at that meeting to arrive at any specific conclusions, but it offered to the foreign ministers of the 15 member nations of NATO an opportunity for consideration of the present international situation and an opportunity to take stock of developments within the alliance. I came away from Copenhagen, Mr. Speaker, with a conviction that the spirit of unity and collaboration within NATO had never been higher than it was at that meeting. It is highly desirable for the success of NATO that there should be developed a spirit of unity within the Atlantic community. There is a great necessity for the maintenance of that spirit of unity and collaboration.
I repeat, it must be the effort of every member of NATO to promote that objective of co-operation. Indeed, since the meeting of the heads of government in Paris in December last year there has been a marked upsurge in consultation, political and otherwise, within NATO. The member nations have consulted readily-and I emphasize the word "readily"-on many grave issues which face us all.
In the last few months the governments of NATO have considered such vital matters as

disarmament, the preparation of agreed views with respect to the many letters that have come from the U.S.S.R., and of course the preparation for a summit meeting or meetings. The degree of confidence which has been developed amongst the NATO allies, as the Prime Minister said the other day, has made it possible for three members of the alliance to act as trusted spokesmen in the conduct of negotiations on certain aspects of preparation for a summit meeting. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this remarkable achievement of such close co-operation as is now being carried out under NATO is a unique development in the history of mankind. Indeed, I use the words of the communique in this regard, "One of the most significant, promising events of our time is the spirit of union within NATO."
During our discussions in Copenhagen there were observations that indicated that there are weaknesses within NATO, and I would mention one particularly. That is in the field of information. It was acknowledged on all sides that NATO as an organization, indeed the member nations of NATO, have not been as successful as the U.S.S.R. in the field of information. Steps will be taken to provide better and improved machinery for the dissemination in factual terms of the views and the actions of NATO and in that way counter the propaganda of the U.S.S.R.
I had the opportunity to observe at the meeting of the foreign ministers, and I do believe and Canada does believe that there can be a greater role for the parliamentarians of the NATO countries. I drew to the attention of the foreign ministers the resolution of the NATO parliamentarians last autumn, sometimes designated as the Kefauver resolution, whereby it was suggested by the parliamentarians that there should be held in 1959 an Atlantic congress to which not only parliamentarians would be invited but also leading citizens in various nations of NATO. I am hopeful that out of plans that are now being studied and laid there will be such a conference to the end that we can get the story of NATO better known to our peoples of the various nations; that there will be an Atlantic conference held about the time of the celebration of the tenth anniversary of the founding of NATO.
On behalf of Canada I emphasized the importance to NATO and to its principal institutions of article II of the treaty. Article II as you know, Mr. Speaker, has to do with economic matters, and I was gratified to receive from many sides of the membership at that meeting the expression of similar views.
The Address-Hon. S. E. Smith We should invoke to a greater degree article II; we should put some flesh on the bones of that article. Undoubtedly there is an opportunity through NATO to promote economic prosperity, notably by-and I emphasize this term; we on this side of the house do not regard it as a naughty one-promoting the expansion of international trade and promoting aid to underdeveloped countries.
Consultation on methods and machinery for implementing the principles set out in article II will take place within the alliance. This does not imply, Mr. Speaker, that we envisage that the NATO council will be the executive organ for economic co-operation. It does seem to me that the best thing NATO could do in this regard would be to study article II and put forward principles, and by reason of or under those principles there could be consultations within the membership of the community and also consultations with international societies and organizations that would be better equipped to consider executive matters. If NATO could implement article II to a greater degree, then undoubtedly, in addition to its military strength, its prestige and influence would be greatly enhanced throughout the world.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to what were to us more vital issues on which consultation took place at the NATO meeting. These related, of course, generally to the international situation confronting the alliance, particularly to the trends of Soviet policy and the attitude the western countries could adopt toward the Soviet union. Exchanges of views in this regard brought about remarkable unanimity of approach on these fundamental issues. We did at the outset agree that some of the recent actions of the U.S.S.R. have raised serious doubts as to the real intention of its leaders regarding a summit meeting. The members of that ministerial meeting of NATO regretted that the Soviet union had aggravated instead of reduced international tensions by its veto in the security council of the proposal put forward by the United States of America relating to the reducing of the risk of a surprise attack over the Arctic area. We also were bound to admit and acknowledge that proposals put forward by the Russians in recent weeks relating to the holding of a meeting, proposals not only of matters of substance but of matters of procedure, had made the preparations for a summit meeting more difficult.
Nevertheless, despite the disappointments and doubts about the Soviet attitude, we

The Address-Hon. S. E. Smith resolved to continue our efforts to pave the way toward a summit meeting. I quote from the communique:
The NATO governments will not be discouraged nor give up their attachment to the principle of negotiation.
It was recognized, however, that while summit meetings are desirable if they offer any reasonable prospect of reaching settlement on fundamental questions, they are not the only way or indeed they may not be the best way of conducting negotiations for the reduction of international tension. A summit meeting could be helpful if it were properly prepared and if it were to take place in a favourable atmosphere.
At the meeting I suggested that the summit meeting, the one for which we have been working through the ambassadors of three members of NATO in Moscow in recent weeks, should be regarded as one of a series of meetings. I suggested, indeed, that it would not necessarily be the first. It could be regarded as the second meeting and we would think of the Geneva meeting in 1955 as the first in that series.
I desire to impress the point upon the house, if I can, that this approach would recognize that it may not be possible-indeed it will not be possible-to settle at one meeting at the summit all the problems which separate the Soviet bloc from the NATO countries. Undoubtedly there has developed in the public opinion of the European members of NATO, and indeed one can sense it in Canada and the United States, a feeling that if we could have a summit meeting we could settle once and for all-some of the suggestions go that far-the problems that separate us from the U.S.S.R.
If we follow the concept of a series of meetings then the next one, the second one as I like to call it, could consider a limited agenda with limited objectives. We could then honestly convey to the public in the various NATO nations that if a question which they naturally would have thought should have been on the agenda of that second meeting was not there it had been postponed to a later meeting. If we have limited objectives and reach a satisfactory reconciliation of the different views in respect of those matters, the smaller items, shall I say, then confidence and trust will be developed in some measure and on the basis of that confidence and trust a further meeting could be called to discuss even more serious questions. Because of the trust and confidence that would have been developed even to a partial degree there would be better prospects for agreement being reached at a subsequent meeting or meetings.


The other day the Leader of the Opposition suggested, and I recognize that he did so tentatively, that the best kind of a meeting at this time might be an informal one between the heads of the United States and the Soviet union for an exchange of views without an agenda. I am unable to share the optimism of the Leader of the Opposition in this regard. While a serious burden of responsibility falls upon the two most powerful nations in the world, nevertheless there are other interests involved on the western side; and that was pointed out the other day in the house by the Prime Minister. Those interests should be adequately represented at a summit meeting. I have in mind that it would be probably unfair to place upon the United States the whole onus or responsibility for conducting negotiations at the summit and to be responsible for the failure of a summit meeting if that were the case.
Also it does occur to me that it would be fruitful to have the heads of the two sides in question meet with an agenda before them. I am not being facetious when I say that I can well see Mr. Khrushchev and Mr. Eisenhower sitting down at a table without an agenda and saying, "What will we discuss now in the field of international tension"? The field of international tension in that context means a global field, and that would call for preparation in order that the participants in such a meeting would be prepared to put forward concrete and considered suggestions. It is my view that such a meeting might not only prove useless but that its failure would increase international tensions rather than reduce them.
At the Copenhagen meeting emphasis was placed on the question of disarmament.

speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, I should like to touch on that later As I said a moment ago, considerable emphasis was placed on the question of disarmament which would, of course, be one of the main items for discussion in any negotiations with the Soviet government. The ministers reaffirmed their view that the proposals of August 29, 1957, in the disarmament commission, the same proposals later being presented to the General Assembly of the United Nations, would form

a reasonable basis for discussion of disarmament, but in reaffirming that view there was what one might well characterize as a note of flexibility.
Pending more general negotiations, however, with respect to disarmament we felt that it might be possible, despite the recent setbacks that have been brought about by the attitude and action of the U.S.S.R., to inaugurate expert technical discussions between representatives of the Soviet union and the western powers principally concerned, such discussions to. cover detailed measures of control over disarmament even though the precise disarmament proposals had not been identified. In discussing this facet of the problem of disarmament we had particularly in mind measures to prevent surprise attack and measures to detect nuclear explosions.
These conclusions were set out in the communique, and they do indicate a degree of flexibility. But in the communique there is also a note of warning to the U.S.S.R. that their recent actions and attitudes have engendered in the west some scepticism as to their real intentions. In view of the uncertainties which exist and the present unfortunate lack of confidence between the Soviet leaders and ourselves, it is conceivable that many of our differences could not be reconciled at the diplomatic table. But we come back to this point, that even if we cannot contemplate reconciliation or settlement with respect to some of these matters, surely this does not dictate that they should not be discussed at some diplomatic level. At the meeting I laid particular stress on behalf of Canada on the need for further consideration of measures for inspection and control. In my opinion such measures are fundamental to any consideration, in any degree, of measures for disarmament. I do believe that measures with respect to control and inspection are fundamental to any disarmament negotiations. Then if we could agree to act with respect to this core problem, confidence would be created and on the basis of that confidence discussions could be held with respect to particular measures for disarmament.
In so far as the west is concerned, and I know I speak for all the members of the house, control means confidence and confidence is lacking at the moment. I proposed on behalf of Canada, and the other foreign ministers agreed, that the council should consider the possibility of carrying out studies and experiments on the technical problems of inspection and control. We recall that first Mr. Bulganin and then Mr. Khrushchev, in reply to letters from Mr. Eisenhower suggesting that there should be experimentation
The Address-Hon. S. E. Smith undertaken for the development of adequate techniques of detection and control, answered in the negative. I did suggest that we might undertake in NATO a pilot scheme for this technical study, and that scheme might be carried out in Canada or in other parts of what one might call the NATO area. If the Russians will not participate in such a joint scheme, the fact that we have initiated it might prompt them to undertake similar .studies in their country. Later we might invite them to exchange information with us, and then we might participate in their scheme and they might participate in ours.
In this connection I am happy to report that there is some hope, as the result of a recent communication from Mr. Khrushchev to Mr. Eisenhower, that the Soviet union would be willing to participate in expert studies into the possible carrying out of an agreement to stop nuclear tests. I know we all hope this note of encouragement might be an indication that the Soviet union would be willing to agree to a similar discussion of the problems of disarmament. If some significant progress could be made in the studies and experimentation with respect to control and supervision of nuclear tests that would provide a notification of the imminence of an attack, then we could move on to some of the more substantive questions.
As I suggested a moment ago, we will have to achieve a better mood of confidence before we can proceed even in that regard, but if we started on the NATO side to undertake studies and experimentation with respect to control and supervision it would be an indication that we are very earnest about that matter, and would indicate to the world our resolution in that regard.
The foreign ministers' meeting at Copenhagen did not consider military matters, which will be considered at the meeting of the NATO council to be held in Paris next December. We did, however, Mr. Speaker, express our satisfaction with the results of the conference of defence ministers which was held in Paris last month. In this regard some of us, and Canada's representative was one of them, expressed the belief that there should be a continued study of the political aspects and implications of our policy and dur decisions in the defence field. This is particularly true if we are to avoid developing rigidities in our political thinking.
Surely the building up and the matching of nuclear weapons by the two sides need not be considered an irrevocable and inevitable process. Where would that inevitable and irrevocable process lead us? It might well lead us to that awful alternative, a catastrophic global war. It is therefore of

The Address-Hon. S. E. Smith paramount importance that we study the relation of our defence position to the position of political negotiations, and it is of paramount importance that we do not lose opportunities to negotiate when the time is ripe and when there is a clear indication of Soviet intentions.
It is difficult for anybody to forecast what the future may hold with respect to discussions with the Soviet union. I am trying to describe the meeting at Copenhagen, and I know we approached that process in a spirit of unity, co-operation and trust within the alliance to which I referred earlier in my remarks. We do wish to avoid provocation and to seek by every possible means to reach agreement with the Soviet leaders. We are not only prepared but we are anxious to negotiate with them at any level, diplomatic or otherwise. I reiterate, however, that if it is a summit meeting there must be much preparation for it.
I come now to the point raised by the Leader of the Opposition. Surely we should not endeavour to prevent the holding of negotiations across the table by reason of procedural matters. Surely if this becomes an important issue in our talks with the U.S.S.R. it should be possible to find a satisfactory formula-I do not know whether this will answer the question that was asked by the Leader of the Opposition-which would not be predicated on the recognition of some far-reaching principle of parity which the Russians have put forward in rather vague terms and which, if introduced into the United Nations, would destroy the effectiveness of that body. Certainly it would lead to a radical transformation of the main organizations of the United: Nations and impair their representative character.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to another important matter. I beg leave to table an exchange of notes between the United States and Canada. They were signed on May 12, one week ago. In this exchange of notes there is to be found the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning the organization and operation of the North American air defence command, which is known as NORAD. Copies of this exchange of notes, I may say for the information of hon. members, are available in the parliamentary distribution office.
In order that I may keep in step with the United States Secretary of State, who will be making a similar announcement this morning in Washington, I am going to carefully follow my notes. Members of the house, Mr. Speaker, will recall that on August 1, 1957, the two governments announced their agreement to the setting up of a system of

integrated operational control of the air defence forces of Canada and the United States. When I speak of Canada and the United States, I mean the country south of our border and also Alaska.
An integrated headquarters was formed shortly after August 1, 1957 and the command has been operating on an interim basis for about nine months. In the light of intensive studies made by expert authorities on the problems of continental air defence and of the experience gained in the past nine months, the Canadian and United States governments have in this exchange of notes registered and recorded formally their understanding of the need for integration of their air defence activities and their agreement on the principles, both military and political, on which the organization and operation of NORAD will be based and indeed have been based during the past nine months.
For the past two decades the co-operation of Canada and the United States in the field of continental defence has grown ever more intimate. Even prior to the formation of NORAD, as many hon. members of this house know, there was close co-operation between the air defence forces of the United States and Canada. That co-ordination arose out of the recognition that the air defence of the two countries had to be thought of as a single problem. Indeed, since 1954 an in-[DOT] tegrated system of air defence has been envisaged and preparations were made for it as early as that year. Recent technological developments had made it obvious to the two governments that co-ordination of national plans was no longer adequate. It is a truism that this globe has become smaller, and one of the main factors in that regard is the reduction in the time it takes to fly from one continent to another. That reduction is salutary and mankind applauds it. But we must never forget the implications of that truism for our defences, and we must construct defences against the possibility of a surprise nuclear attack. We must therefore have in existence in peacetime an organization which, in the face of surprise attack, could immediately take defensive action over our own territories in accordance with a single air defence plan which had already been approved by the two governments.
The integration, I would remind the house, is the practical application of the principle of interdependence within NATO. This integration will contribute to the effectiveness of the air defence of this continent. It will also increase the ability of Canada and the United States to meet the strategic objectives

established in NATO, after the setting up of the Canada-United States region under NATO. The effectiveness of such integration has been amply demonstrated in other NATO areas. I am thinking of Canadians who are now under the command of SACEUR, the supreme allied commander in Europe. I am thinking of Canadians who are serving under SACLANT, the supreme allied commander, Atlantic. There are other areas under NATO where there is an integrated command. I am thinking of the allied forces, central Europe, and the allied forces, Mediterranean, in which Canada is not represented.
Our joint defence of the continent cannot, of course, be thought of in isolation. This continental effort forms part of our contribution to NATO defences. The Canada-United States region which was established under NATO is an integral part or indeed an integrated part of NATO; and as I said a moment ago, the establishment of this integrated operational command known as NORAD will contribute to the strategic objectives set for the Canada-United States region in NATO and will assist our two governments to meet these objectives more effectively.

I am certain we all listened to the speech with a great deal of interest; it is the longest I ever heard in my five years here and my 20 years in British Columbia. One of the main outcomes of the speech will, I hope, be a recognition by the Prime Minister and his cabinet that promises are not fulfilled, nor are problems met, merely by the early introduction of emergency legislation. It is very welcome as far as it goes, but it is of the utmost importance to the people of Canada that emergency legislation in these fields be extended by the introduction of more comprehensive legislation at an early date, even though it may be delayed to some extent.
May I very briefly say, as has been stated by other members of this group, that we welcome the change in the Unemployment Insurance Act, but that it is imperative that the entire act be overhauled so as to effectively provide for the unemployed in all seasons and at all levels. All of us who are members of this House of Commons, irrespective of party, if we are honest in our opinions and our principles must realize that we cannot possibly rest content while we have an Unemployment Insurance Act covering only just over 60 per cent of the unemployed persons in Canada, and which in times of stress covers only one season without recognizing the fact that unemployment, whether it be great or small, can occur at any time and even many times in the year to the same person, according to his occupation.
I very much want to stress my opinion that the introduction of the emergency legislation is no solution to the unemployment problem, and must be followed by a complete overhauling of the act at an early date.

Mr. Speaker, at the time of adjournment I was drawing the attention of the Prime Minister and the government to the absolute necessity of carrying into effect the statement in the speech from the throne regarding action to establish secondary industries in Canada. I pointed out that immediate action was required. I mentioned an example in the province of British Columbia involving two cities of which we are proud, namely Fernie and Britannia. I am not going to continue with that matter at the present time, as another opportunity will undoubtedly arise later in this session.
However, with respect to the matter of secondary industries, we have to consider the position of Canada generally and that of the provinces in particular. Our country is generally dependent on export trade and the province of British Columbia particularly so. For over a year now British Columbia has been very severely hit by the loss of our traditional markets for our base metals, our pulp and general timber products.
This brings to mind something which I think it is very necessary to draw to the attention of the government at this time. Speaking particularly now of my own province of British Columbia, may I say that in the past few months our predicament as far as employment is concerned has come about to some extent-I say only to some extent- because we have been undercut in our traditional markets for base metals and timber products. This has been done, and I repeat only to some extent, by a new economic 57071-3-13*
The Address-Mr. Winch policy of the U.S.S.R. In the past year we have been undercut by that country on base metals and in the case of aluminum particularly to the extent of approximately 2 cents a pound. We have also been undercut on our timber exports. Without particularizing I will merely say that we now see the U.S.S.R. entering into a new phase of world diplomacy, a phase involving economic or trade manoeuvring, a policy that can have very serious results as far as Canada is concerned as an exporting country, although in the long run it may have beneficial aspects otherwise.
In the past year a number of Canadian businessmen visited the U.S.S.R. and according to the information I have received they state that Russia's logging industry is as efficient as that on the west coast of Canada, where we have prided ourselves as being very efficient, and that the sawmill end of the industry is possibly even more efficient. From what we have heard from these businessmen, and this is what I want to emphasize, Russia is spending approximately ten times as much as Canada on research per tree cut and per thousand board feet processed.
I do not have the time to go into all the implications of this new economic, trade and diplomatic policy, but as a citizen of Canada and a representative of the people of the country I do say that I feel personally it is necessary for the government to face up to the realities of the present trade situation. The government should face up to the reality of our loss of British Columbia markets for our base metals, particularly aluminum, and our timber products, and should recognize that we have definitely reached a time when, although basically the responsibility should rest on industry with regard to research, efficiency and other matters, the federal government should, in the interests of maintaining employment and the trading economy of the nation, speedily announce greatly increased allotments in the field of research as far as industrial operations are concerned.
I want to emphasize in this regard that I think the government will be derelict in its responsibilities if it does not take a realistic approach to the matter and during the present session enunciate major policies and allocate large amounts of money to assist our provinces and industries in the field of research in order to enable us, operating under a capitalist system, to maintain employment through the medium of the export of our products.
There is only one other phase of the speech from the throne to which I should like to draw the attention of the government and

The Address-Mr. Winch the house. I believe that certain incidents of the past few days and, indeed, throughout the past year make it almost mandatory on the government to make its position clear with regard to Canadian control of our own policies and our own economy. To put the matter in blunt language, I think the government must now make it explicitly and implicitly clear that it is not going to be prone to deference to the United States. Deference to our powerful neighbour to the south must not give way to subservience either in the international field or with regard to our own economic policies.
I think it is important to our country that there be policy statements and, if required, legislation so it may be made clear to the people of Canada in particular and of the United States that Canada controls its own destiny, its own international and economic policies. It must be made clear to the people of Canada particularly that there is no longer going to be subservience to United States companies that may own or control subsidiary companies in Canada from the point of view of their directing whether or not we can produce and sell to other countries.
I refer, of course, in particular to the reported incident in which Canada was not permitted to sell automobiles to China because of a United States law. I say, sir, that this is our country and no matter where companies are owned which are operating in our country, on our natural resources and on the wealth poduced by our people, it must be made clear, by legislation if necessary, that we in Canada sell where we desire to sell.
As a corollary to that I want to add my support to the words so eloquently expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West concerning the recognition of China. I feel very strongly on that subject. I said in a campaign speech before March 31, and I repeat on the floor of this house, that I am afraid Canada is still maintaining a position which is known agriculturally under a cer-so much from hon. members of the government over a long period of time concerning their love, loyalty and admiration for the United Kingdom that I suggest to them that when it comes to recognition of China, perhaps they should have long ago followed the tain definition. I am convinced that some cloudy day for Canada, but a bright day for the United States, the United States will announce recognition of China and already have a settled basis for trade. We have heard lead of the United Kingdom. I feel that we in Canada should not drag behind the United States, but should follow the lead of the United Kingdom and recognize China on an

ambassadorial basis, and enter immediately into negotiations to our mutual benefit in the trade situation.
I have spoken about a number of matters during this debate. I recognize that my time is coming to a close. I have spoken in the main in generalities, but I hope I have been able to enunciate the principles which I personally, and I think I can safely say our group collectively, feel are of importance at this time. We hope to have an opportunity in the not too distant future to discuss these broad, general principles in detail.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that although we are a small group in this corner we have the same feelings of loyalty and understanding to our country as do the members of any other party. There are three parties in this house, two of them holding the same fundamental principles. We believe in the necessity for a fundamental change; but believing in democracy we will, as representatives in this house, do our utmost at all times to assist in constructive measures that will be of benefit to our country, to the people in general, to our provinces and constituencies.
I want to take this opportunity of publicly, in the House of Commons, thanking the supporters of Vancouver East, because, in my ninth election campaign, they thought I would make a good representative here. I wish to assure them that I shall at all times put forward constructive criticism and constructive measures.

first words, of course, Mr. Speaker, must be to concur in everything that has been said about you, and in particular to congratulate you, sir, upon achieving such favourable comment after such a hectic time during what, I suppose, is now going to be called the short parliament. I can further assure them that Disraeli was correct when he said of the British house that it was the most chilling and nerve-destroying audience in the world.

If I may be placed for a moment in the category of one making a maiden speech, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something about the vast riding of York-Scarborough which I have the privilege of representing in this house. The first thing that must be said about this riding concerns an important father of confederation who, I am sure, is whirling in his grave somewhere in Toronto. I refer, of course, to George Brown, that great advocate of representation by population. In York-Scarborough today there are approximately
200,000	people. By 1962, at which time it will be possible to bring about redistribution, according to a conservative estimate there will be between 325,000 and 350,000 people in that constituency. It will be apparent immediately that York-Scarborough is not adequately represented in this house-

I have made inquiries privately amongst the law officers and other agencies in a position to advise me, and I am told that I am at the mercy of the house in any attempt to achieve some relief in terms of trying- and I underline the word "trying"-to represent adequately that many people. The physical proportions of the riding of York-Scarborough are simply described by a line drawn through Yonge street and No. 11 highway, which roughly bisects the city of Toronto and sweeps around eastward to the lake. Within the boundaries of this area lies most of the open land available for building to take up the outward growth of the city.
I think it is fair to say that of every two new houses built in the metropolitan Toronto area one will be built in York-Scarborough.
Not too many years ago the riding of York-Scarborough was a pleasant countryside on the perimeter of Toronto. Starting with the war and gathering momentum following the war an invasion of massive proportions took place. An example of the numbers involved I can give to you in this fashion. Between the election in 1953 and the election in 1957
The Address-Mr. McGee
100,000	people moved into that riding; and of course with the inspired policies of this government this pace has increased. Between the election of last June and the election in March there were 9,000 more voters on the voters' lists.
Following this massive invasion of people- mostly young people with young families moving into their own homes for the first time- came an accompanying movement of industry following the labour force and personnel to the suburban areas, resulting in such dynamic areas as the golden mile, to say nothing of Leaside and North York. But what is most important about the riding of York-Scarborough is the people who live within its boundaries. They are good citizens conscientious in the discharge of their civic duties at the municipal, provincial and federal level.
As an example of good citizenship in action may I point out that during the last campaign their were no fewer than 15 joint meetings to which all candidates of all parties were invited for general debate, equal time being allowed and a question period following. In addition there were 150 neighbourhood meetings to which I was invited. That is an example of a people interested, concerned and willing to participate in the functioning of democracy in this country. I have not the figures at hand, but it is my understanding that the percentage of people who voted in that riding is as high as any in the Dominion of Canada.
There has been some discussion about the results of this election, and some reasons have been advanced as to why the result was as it was. The leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Assiniboia, summed it all up in simple words. He said the only reason the Conservatives formed the government was that many people were saying, "Should we not give the government a chance?" or "Let us give John a chance"; that it was just as simple as that.
I have a few comments which will indicate that it was not as simple as that by any means. In my opinion the reason stems first from the fact that the Conservative party had the dynamic and dramatic leadership of the Prime Minister. In the second place this government, which was a minority government, faced a most difficult economic situation and a rather more difficult political situation.	The verdict of the people, as I
recognize it, was that it had done an excellent job, not just that it deserved another chance but that it had to have it.
The fourth reason for the result which obtained is, I suggest, that in their own way each of the other parties in contesting this

The Address-Mr. McGee election made presentations and submissions to the people of Canada most of which added up to an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian voter. I refer to examples of candidates, some of whom were returned and others who were not, stumping the country and screaming that Tory times are hard times. One of them even went into an historical treatise to establish this preposterous nonsense, and it was interpreted as such by most of the electorate. In Toronto we had such extreme statements on the front pages of our newspapers as one saying that Tory policies were stupid and dishonest. We had suggestions that the government was antiAmerican, as well as many other wild statements which could not be supported. Certainly in York-Scarborough the voters gave their answer to such suggestions and accorded me a majority which I understand is larger than any previous one in history.
As to the debate thus far and the amendment involving economic planning may I say in spite of what the hon. member for Essex East stated:
. . . this government has not given any evidence of a program designed to meet this national problem of unemployment in Canada at this time.
And the Leader of the Opposition's statement:
The word "recession" is not mentioned. It is a bad word, apparently, which must not be used.
In spite of statements such as those, Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that this government has given Canada a new position in world affairs. I suggest that Canada leads all countries in the world in terms of anti-recession legislation. Policies which were orginated by this government are now being discussed in the United States at great length. Statements appeared during the election emanating from my opponent in my riding and from his leaders throughout the country that this was not so. If I may very quickly review the matter in detail I should like to do so. It seems to me that government action on an anti-recession basis should evolve in two ways; first, government anti-recession action should put more money into the hands of the people. Certainly this is fundamental economic theory. It should further, if possible, put that money into the hands of people who need that money and, of course it follows, who will spend it.
In that regard I should like to list briefly the things that were done. They include the old age pension increase, the old age assistance increase, payments to disabled persons extended, the blind pension increased, veterans allowances and benefits, disability pension benefits; money put into the hands of people

who needed that money and who would spend it, putting more money in circulation and certainly creating more purchasing power.
Beyond that, the obvious method of putting more money back into the pockets of people in this country was by tax reductions, $146 million worth. Again what I liked best about this method-and certainly it was reflected in the reaction of the voters in my riding-was that they started substantially at the bottom, giving relief where it was most needed, in the lower income brackets. Certainly as far as increased tax deduction for children was concerned, this was greeted with much enthusiasm in my riding, which has more young children than any three normal ridings in this country. Other money was put into circulation to create purchasing power and economic activity through cash advances on farmstored grain and financial assistance to the provinces.
In addition to taking action to inject more money into the bloodstream of the economy, the government took further action by accelerating the public works program and moving forward starting dates on government-sponsored projects in order to create more jobs. Even more important as far as my own riding is concerned, and as far as I personally am concerned, was the action taken in the last parliament and continued in this parliament by the Minister of Public Works to expand the house building program. Those
9,000	voters I mentioned who moved into York-Scarborough between last June and March of this year moved largely into homes built under legislation brought in by this government last year. My Liberal opponent experienced difficulty in sustaining his point that this government was doing nothing, when around us on every side, in every area of the riding, was a rate of home building double or treble the rate established in the winter months a year before.
No policy for the recession? No anti-recession activities? I refer to the speech from the throne, and draw the attention of hon. members to the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act and the relief attendant thereto; to the increased rate of house building which I have mentioned; to the substantial public investment and to the expansion of public works in the north, all of which are part and parcel of the steps the government has taken to deal with this situation.
I should like for one moment to look at the situation in the United States in more detail, and to compare it with our own. A debate has been going on for something like seven months south of the border on whether or not taxes should be cut. The administration has been asking, "If we cut taxes will people save the money or spend it?" and so on. We in Canada began cutting taxes well

back in last year. I suppose it is the privilege of a backbencher to make guesses like anybody else in this country, and I suggest we may yet be cutting taxes some more.
In the United States the debate goes on concerning whether or not government spending should be increased. Well, Mr. Speaker, our government began its program in this regard some time ago. We started last October with unemployment insurance compensation, housing projects and so on; and on a comparable basis we have done five times as much as the United States in housing loans. The economies of the United States and Canada are so tied together that I believe there will never be a situation where one country is in the state of recession while the other is in a state of inflation. We may move upward and downward at varying rates, but substantially we will be in the same phase. I would encourage the government of the United States to take an example from the leadership which I mentioned a few moments ago and accelerate its program as we are accelerating ours in order to bring about a continental economic situation which is so vital.
I should like now to say something about the national pastime of suggesting what the federal government should do. Across my desk as, I know, across the desks of most hon. members flows an avalanche of material from every quarter-industry, labour, and every known organization-giving suggestions and ideas as to what the federal government should do. I have an idea that perhaps the responsibility for the economic future of this country does not lie exclusively within the federal realm, and I hope that when the Minister of Labour convenes his conference of labour, management and industry, out of that meeting will come a progressive and aggressive move on the part of labour and on the part of industry to pitch in and help us dig ourselves out of this recession.
I would certainly look to labour, and the housing industry particularly, which has benefited tremendously from the expansion in this area of our economy, to come forward with a program which, I am sure, will be looked on with favour by this government, to bring about a solution to our winter unemployment problem.
We have had a lot of experience in fighting recessions in this country; we have a recession every winter. I should like to see a plan, long term and short term, involving public works-public works which before this government took office did not exist-coordinated with the building industry and with labour to bring about a sort of public works
The Address-Mr. McGee anti-recession measure each winter, a move which would certainly answer a social need.
Technological methods of solving the difficulties of building during the winter have advanced tremendously in the past few years. In my own riding there is a development plan to accommodate 30,000 people. Certain impediments exist which prevent this work being started. I would urge the government and the Minister of Public Works to take what action may be necessary to remove these impediments in order that next winter, the following winter and the year after that construction may go ahead on this project.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier that during the recent election campaign charges of anti-Americanism were levelled against the government. In his speech the Leader of the Opposition mentioned at the outset something about telling our best customers things they were not too happy to hear. I used to be a buyer in my civilian occupation, and in that capacity I used to buy considerable amounts from various sources. On many occasions it became necessary for me to go to a good customer and move some of the contracts planned to be placed with that manufacturer to another in order to protect myself as a buyer and protect my company from the situation which might arise from having too many eggs in one basket. In fact the suggestion made in my riding during the election was that we should have followed such a policy, but not told the Americans that this was the intention.
I have always believed in my own dealings -and I think they should apply also to government dealings on an international plane- that such things should be done openly and not behind people's backs, and if one is facing a new situation with regard to the balance of trade it is better, in my view, to say so frankly.
With regard to this charge of anti-Americanism I should like to refer the house to an editorial which appeared yesterday in the New York Times. Referring to a suggestion in some quarters of an anti-American nationalism in Canada, the editorial says;
This is a distortion. Canadian "nationalism." so-called, is prideful, honest and healthy. No right-minded citizen of this country could deplore it. It will bring grievances to the surface, and that is all to the good. That is as it should be between close friends. Probably we need, here in the United States, a greater flexibility in some of our policies. Probably Canada needs a better understanding of what we are trying to do.
This I suggest is the answer, or part of it, to such criticisms.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to outline my specific ambition in this House of Commons. It is simply this; that

The Address-Mr. Robichaud after I depart, through choice or otherwise, it may be said of me that I was a good member. I do not think there is any more worthy ambition for anyone coming into this house. The only promise I have made in two election campaigns, and the promise I now make to you, sir, and to this house, is that I will do my very best. I do not think anyone can or should promise more.

From now on, Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes at my disposal my remarks will be restricted to or at least very closely connected with, the program enunciated in the speech from the thone. The Prime Minister, as is outlined in the speech from the throne, is asking parliament to direct its attention to these things which are considered necessary and of immediate importance to the people of Canada.
We members of this house, irrespective of party affiliation and whether sitting with the government or the opposition, have a responsibility to protect the rights of the people and at the same time assure a high level of employment and prosperity in our country. There are certain measures therefore which we believe are necessary and of immediate importance in order to benefit the people of Canada.
We have learned from the speech from the throne that all the countries of the commonwealth have accepted the Canadian proposal that a commonwealth trade and economic conference be held in Montreal in September of this year. We certainly welcome such an announcement, but unfortunately we have good reasons to be rather sceptical about the result of any such conference. The people of Canada have not yet forgotten the Mont Tremblant conference which was termed "a great flop" when the British had prepared very thoroughly for that meeting while our Canadian representatives went to the conference as though they had forgotten about their homework. Will the policy of the government at this coming conference be governed by a straight diversion of 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to Britain, or will it be based on more solid ground such a higher and expanding level of international trade with all countries, as we enunciated in the amendment moved by our leader, the hon. member for Algoma East?
When employment for all should be the main concern of every member of this house, when unemployment figures are from 75 per cent to 80 per cent higher today than in May of last year, we are told in the speech from the throne that this parliament will be asked to enact a new bill of rights to safeguard the rights of all persons in Canada in respect of all subjects within the jurisdiction of parliament. We realize that we have in such a bill a dream, a vision highly cherished by the Prime Minister himself, but we must also admit that we Canadians have enjoyed since the early days of our constitution a maintenance and preservation of

freedom probably unequalled in any other free country of the world.
I would therefore suggest to the Prime Minister and to the other members of the present government that precedence be given to more urgent matters, matters which concern the immediate welfare and general economy of the Canadian people. The constitution of Canada established in the British North America Act safeguards the rights of all Canadian citizens irrespective of racial origin; and all Canadians are proud of this act which has given us, as I have just said, a freedom probably unequalled in any other free country.
Speaking of a bill of rights, I might mention that listening this morning to the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs I felt that what we now need is a bill of rights for parliament, when such a military alliance as the one announced by that minister this morning should be considered by parliament and should not rest upon the shoulders of the present government without consulting with parliament as a whole.
There is another aspect of the speech from the throne which I would like to mention, and that has to do with a matter which concerns all of us in this house at the present time; that is, sustained employment for all together with accelerated development of our natural resources. The government has decided on what it calls a major program of useful public works projects and the encouragement of the development and processing of our natural resources. However, as has been said before by members of the opposition who preceded me in this debate, there is very little new in this so-called huge public works program launched by the government, the major portion of which was outlined in detail in the estimates for the fiscal year 1958-1959 tabled on Tuesday last. The works projects totalling $280 million during the first quarter of 1958 and $1,185 million for the full calendar year, a large part of which is for the government's so-called natural development policy, will certainly not meet the objective of the government of removing the dark cloud of unemployment which is presently spreading over Canada from coast to coast, and which may be more apparent in the Atlantic provinces than in any other section of the country. It is, moreover, a recognized fact that the largest share of these public works projects included in the present estimates are but a continuation or completion of projects started by the previous government.
We from the Atlantic provinces are not against such projects of major importance as
The Address-Mr. Robichaud the South Saskatchewan dam and the Pine Point railway in the far north. We understand that the politically-minded Prime Minister could not resist implementing certain of his promises to that effect, but this does not prove to us and to the country in general that such projects are economically sound and urgently needed at this particular time of recession. The program of building new roads in the northern territories to develop the wealth of mineral resources could have some economic justification; but just the same all hon. members, and particularly the members of the present government, should take a second look at some of the announcements made by the Prime Minister, such as the one made in Prince Albert to the effect that he had in mind a road 212 miles long from Prince Albert to Flin Flon and also a 550-mile road from Lac La Ronge to Uranium City on lake Athabaska.
We are not against future development of this country from north to south through a policy of access roads, making available the vast resources of the northern section of Canada, but we all understand also that new roads are urgently needed right now in some of the other provinces in areas already well populated, and where they could benefit already established and operating industries. We know what new roads would mean to the tourist industry in the Atlantic provinces and the additional revenue it would bring to our population.
We would therefore ask the Prime Minister before it is too late to reconsider his northern vision and give due consideration not only to a western vision, as was mentioned this morning by the hon. member for Vancouver East, but also to an eastern vision to include the other provinces of Canada.
We are not against the so-called specific $75 million development at Frobisher bay on Baffin island. We recognize that Canada is a growing country with great possibilities and prospects for future development; but at the same time it is our duty as members of the opposition to suggest to this government the right kind of planning in conjunction with a tax policy which will improve the present wavering economy of the country.
We are aware of the vast mineral resources of the Arctic region. We know that the whole of the Northwest Territories, with its 1,300,000 square miles, offers new ground for important economic developments in the years to come. However, we must admit that right now, in the month of May, 1958, hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens, in fact most probably over 500,000 of them, are seeking work which they urgently need. We recall those words of the Prime Minister,

The Address-Mr. Robichaud only mention of fisheries was made in the following very few words:
Unremitting efforts are being made to sell Canadian agricultural and fisheries products in the markets of the world-[DOT]
There is no doubt in my mind that the fishing industry today is experiencing its own particular difficulties. Our Atlantic coast fishermen are being paid today for their fish prices which do not keep pace with the national economy. Prices for fish are in many instances even lower than they were 8 or 10 years ago. What are the main reasons for this unfavourable situation? Is it disorderly marketing by our processors and dealers combined with too much emphasis by governments on production and conservation alone?
The fishing industry is facing problems today which should be attacked vigorously if the industry is to survive and prosper. Governments, both federal and in the provinces concerned, should give, in co-operation with the industry, more attention to marketing and at the same time establish a sound program of sales promotion, advertising and education. There is no reason whatsoever why in some areas of the Atlantic provinces our fishermen should be paid less than 3 cents per pound for their fresh cod delivered at landing points.
It is not my intention at this time to make elaborate remarks on the fishing industry. My time is limited by the rule of debate and I will have other occasions to discuss this matter in much more detail. The fishing industry, however, is one of major importance on the east and west coasts of our country and deserves the full attention of the government. I want to warn the government that the fishing industry has some definite reservations on the question of a firmer stand on trade with the United States, and one must not forget that one-half of Canada's fisheries products, to a value of $90 million annually, are consumed in the United States. The government will also be asked to give more serious attention to the declining Atlantic salt fish industry which is seriously affected by the loss of important international markets together with higher costs of production.
Notwithstanding the statement made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) in Halifax a few weeks ago to the effect that the industry should not be concerned with the recent curtailment of import quotas on fresh and frozen fillets by the United States government, we of the opposition feel that the possible consequences to the fishing industry of the government's stand on trade matters with the United States should be carefully weighed before proceeding further

in this direction. We are aware of the efforts made on previous occasions by the United States fishing industry to curtail fish imports. We know what the acceptance by the United States government of the United States tariff commission recommendations would mean to our fishing industry and there is no need for us to emphasize further that the diversion trade policy of the government is creating disquietude and fear among our own fish exporters.
We do not want further curbs on imports of fishery products by United States authorities, and again we are asking the government to exercise definite reservations in its attitude towards our United States neighbours, in order to protect an industry which is so vital to the economy of the Atlantic provinces.
There are many other problems facing the fishing industry today which I should like to bring to the attention of this house, but I shall reserve my remarks for a later date when I may have an opportunity of dealing exclusively with fisheries problems.
Since the opening of the present session, the house has approved amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, extending seasonal benefits to June 28, for this year only. This, we understood, was but a temporary, emergency measure to take partial care of the exceptionally large number of unemployed at a period when usually employment should be at least normal. If unemployment insurance has been introduced to protect labour during a period of unemployment in this country, the act should be amended to cover farm employees who certainly deserve protection.
In conclusion, 1 express the hope that the government will see its way clear to introduce, during the present session, amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which would include benefits for employees on our Canadian farms.
