Mr. Speaker, as a freshman, I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating you upon the high position to which you have been elevated. I should like also to extend congratulations to the Deputy Speaker and the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At this time I should like to refer back 22 years to a time when Harry J. Barber, of Chilliwack, was the last Progressive Conservative member to represent the Fraser valley district in this house. I had a letter from him yesterday and he is just as much interested today as he was then in the doings of this great parliament.
I propose to locate for you, Mr. Speaker, the Fraser Valley constituency, and then I

should like to take a few moments to outline some of the problems that we have in the Fraser valley. Before doing this, however, I should like to say that this is the centennial year for British Columbia. Those of you who have visited the province during the last month or two might wonder what it was that you saw walking around the streets of our cities and towns with large beards, mustaches, sideburns and so on. These people represent what human beings looked like some one hundred ago. In addition to that, our ladies love to go out dressed in the long skirts with the hoops, the large hats, and even in Chilliwack, the largest town in our district, it is quite the proper thing for every lady on Friday to go out dressed in such costumes. I trust, too, that whenever any district in British Columbia asks for help in celebrating this centennial year, this government will see fit to do what it can to help.
The Fraser Valley constituency which I represent extends from about Cisco Lodge in the northeast corner, up the Fraser valley canyon on both sides of the river for about 150 miles, and then west to Aldergrove on the south side of the Fraser river, and to the Pitt river which runs into the Fraser on the north side. During the last election there were some 40,000 voters in the area. This is a very important tourist area and includes some very scenic routes, particularly the one down the Fraser valley canyon with the rugged mountains showing on each side. In some areas the highway circles around the mountain tops quite high from the bottom of the Fraser valley canyon. I have known several instances of our prairie neighbours, who are used to driving on the level, really getting the jitters when they are driving around some of these mountain peaks away up in the heavens.
This Fraser canyon has in it Hell's Gate, at which point there are salmon ladders to allow the salmon to go up the Fraser river to the spawning grounds. When the water rises three or four feet during flood time at Hell's Gate it has little effect on the water level farther down where the Fraser river spreads out to a considerable width. The Harrison Hot Springs spa is also one of the tourist attractions in the Fraser river valley. Here, of course, is the Agassiz experimental farm, which is one of the original experimental farms started in 1888. It is in the shade of Mount Cheam, one of the beautiful mountains of the area. At this time of the year, as the snow melts, one can see the form of an angel outlined in the snow on the side of Mount Cheam, and that is known as the guardian angel of the Fraser valley.
The Address-Mr. Hicks
In this area there is a great deal of commercial fishing between the Pattullo bridge, which is in New Westminster, and the Mission City bridge. There has been some concern amongst local fishermen, who have been living on small farms and fishing during the season, because the season has been curtailed lately. Last year closure was put on in this area from September 15, and the fishermen felt this was a hardship. There is also some mining in this area, particularly in the Hope area on the south side of the Fraser. There is some small mining done on the north shore. From Lytton down the Fraser valley to the extreme western end, there is commercial logging and lumbering. There are some quite large mills operating in the Hope, Mission, Chilliwack, Haney and other areas, cutting lumber for the local and export trade. There are also many smaller mills in the area. These are important business concerns and certainly add a great deal to the employment opportunities and resources of the area.
Agriculture, however, is our main resource in the Fraser valley, and is the thing about which I am mostly concerned. It includes such crops as peas, corn and the small fruits like strawberries and raspberries for canning and freezing. Also of great importance from an agricultural standpoint is the poultry business, including not only the turkey breeding work but also the raising of poultry for meat and egg production. Growers in my constituency are thankful for the assistance given the turkey growers last fall when the United States turkeys were being dumped into the area. The poultry industry in this area almost equals in value the dairy industry. These two branches of agriculture in the Fraser Valley constituency are almost identical with the same crops from the edge of the Fraser Valley constituency to the coast. This area is in the New Westminster riding including Langley, Cloverdale, Ladner and so on. The poultry and dairy industries combined provide over 50 per cent of the cash value of the farms in the province of British Columbia. The large Fraser valley milk producers association, a co-operative that operates mostly in the Fraser valley, sold $25,580,597 worth of products last year. That will give you some idea of the importance of this great co-operative organization.
I should now like to take a few minutes to mention some of the problems of the constituency with which I have been, shall I say, bombarded since March 31. You might be surprised to learn that this whole area which 1 have mentioned, even right down to the Ladner area which goes right to the coast, is extremely short of domestic water. Where the rainfall is so heavy and where the Fraser river runs through the centre of it,

The Address-Mr. Hicks one would be inclined to think that the domestic water supply should be quite appropriate for the need. However, such is not the case. Almost every one of these areas is concerned about the domestic water supply, probably not so much for today but rather because they foresee what is coming in the years ahead, particularly as people are moving in in larger and larger numbers all the time.
Some considerable work has been done in engineering and in making inquiries of all kinds in connection with trapping water from tributaries which run into the Vedder river southeast of Chilliwack. As this water comes down off the mountains from glaciers up on top, it is wonderful water, with no contamination whatever. If it could be put into large pipes and run right down through the centre of the Fraser valley and sold to each of the municipalities as it goes by, it would help a great deal not only in the Chilliwack area but in Sumas prairie, which is a dike farming area with very wonderful land, and also in Aldergrove and in Matsqui municipality and further on down to the coast outside of the Fraser Valley constituency which I represent. The Elk Creek water works of Chilliwack are the people who supply Chilliwack with its water at the present time and they are having trouble in getting an adequate supply. In this same area is a large army camp of the Canadian engineers. Water must be supplied to it.
There are two tributaries running into the Vedder river. Incidentally the Vedder river is not suitable for damming because it goes on the rampage at flood time, so much so that engineers assert that it could not be dammed and handled properly. But there are, in fact, three tributaries running into it, with almost ready made places where dams could easily be put in. I know of no other one thing in my constituency or even in the Fraser valley as a whole that would give more satisfaction, more happiness or more pleasure to all the people therein than an adequate supply of fresh clean water. It could be used for domestic purposes in all the homes and it could also be used at certain seasons of the year for irrigation purposes on farm land.
Next I should like to mention the fact that I was invited to a council meeting in Haney not long before I left home. The Haney reeve is chairman of the mosquito control area there. They wondered whether more funds could not be secured from the federal government in order to assist, particularly in this centennial year, in controlling mosquitoes. Of course this matter has to do with all municipalities in the Fraser valley. I


understand the amount last year was $1,500. They should like to see that amount doubled.
Let me mention some of the problems of some of the other municipalities. Incidentally may I say that in some of my campaign talks I mentioned the fact that I would, if elected, try to keep in touch as much as possible with the municipal officers in the particular riding. By doing that one can keep in touch with the individuals as well. Just recently the teamsters strike was concluded in British Columbia and this meant a great deal to the situation that had arisen in the Hope area which exists mostly on the tourist trade and lumbering. Nothing with regard to lumbering could be done there until the teamsters strike was settled.
Then as to Chilliwack, I mentioned the army camp there. They are looking for larger grants to their municipality, not forgetting and expressing thanks for what has been supplied previously. According to the information given to me, in 1955 there was a $13,159 grant to the municipality of Chilliwack; in 1956 it was $12,537. When I left they had not had word as to what the 1957 grant would be, but they hoped it would amount to $20,000. The trans-Canada highway runs through this municipality and they would hope that work on this project could be started immediately. On the north side of the river in Kent municipality they are desirous of having the highway completed as a civil defence project, if for no other reason.
The Mission municipality, which also would benefit by this water supply that I mentioned some time ago, have a project which they should like to see developed, that is 100 acres being diked along the river bank and filled in, as apparently some company is endeavouring to purchase this site for industrial purposes. This, of course, would be a wonderful thing, something similar to what is being done on Annasis island at the present time.
Matsqui municipality has a large airport which will be better known to hon. members as Abbotsford airport. This airport extends over some 1,200 acres, and the people feel that the assessment value of $3.50 per acre placed on it by the federal government is too low. They would like to see it increased.
All municipalities in my area are, of course, looking forward to assistance and help from the government toward their education programs. Apparently the provincial government is financially unable to supply all the requirements, and the municipalities are therefore looking to the federal government for some assistance in this regard.

Another matter which is important to the constituency which I represent and to the area further down between the Fraser valley and the coast is the feed situation as it affects poultry men and livestock growers in that area. I believe that those interested have no quarrel with the Canadian wheat board regulations which set the price for milling wheat, but it does not seem fair to the poultry and livestock men in British Columbia that wheat can be purchased by one farmer from another, or by feeders directly from farmers on the prairies at between 50 cents to 65 cents a bushel for the lower grades while the price a producer has to pay directly the grain crosses the mountains is three times that sum, up to $50 a ton, which is the way feed is sold in British Columbia. Poultry and livestock men in British Columbia have to compete with the prairie producers of poultry products as well as with imports from the state of Washington. It is admitted, of course, that there is a freight subsidy on this feed coming into British Columbia, but it would still be a wonderful thing for the province if something could be done.
Another problem, and one which is, I understand, being looked after at the present time at least as far as strawberry production is concerned, is raised by the dumping of berries into British Columbia from the state of Washington at very low prices. There will be something like 3,000 tons of raspberries for export from the Fraser valley this year, but there will be imports of strawberries also on account of the frost which a few years ago killed a lot of the plants.
These are some of the major problems we face in the Fraser valley.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a great pleasure to join with other hon. members of this house and congratulate you upon your election as speaker of the twenty-fourth parliament. I know that as a scholar and a gentleman you will maintain the rights and privileges of the minority groups in this chamber. In the tradition of this house I should like also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I think it might serve some purpose if in these fast changing times when each day the morning newspaper screams new headlines at us I were to take a little time to discuss the really remarkable change and development which has taken place in our political system and in our thinking since the time of confederation. There is no need for me to stress the economic strides made by this country; the fact that we have become the
19, 1958
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton fourth trading nation in the world is sufficient evidence of this growth. I should prefer to limit these few words to a discussion of Canada and the commonwealth, and to a new appraisal of the commonwealth. I should like to refer to the uniqueness of the Canadian position both geographically and historically and to the consequent opportunities in foreign policy that this gives us generally.
It seems to me that the Canadian attitude toward the commonwealth has undergone very great changes in the past 50 years, and I think it may be said that from confederation in 1867 down to 1914 the principal struggle was how to convert responsible government and confederation into real working internal and external sovereignty for all effective purposes. That question was largely solved by the realities of the first world war. We entered into a second phase of Canadian political development in the celebrated imperial conferences which were held in 1926 and 1931. Hon. members will remember the Balfour declaration of 1926-"free and autonomous nations, no one subordinate to the other"- and the 1931 Imperial conference which resulted in the Statute of Westminster.
I think it is fair to say that the nineteen twenties and nineteen thirties were marked by a growing body of Canadian opinion more detached from commonwealth sentiment than before. This was probably due to an anxiety to express our new found independence in the fullest possible way. However, during the period between 1939 and 1945, the period of world war II, I think we learned the full meaning of sovereignty with all its attendant responsibilities; I think we came to realize that the mother country would, in time of crisis, depend to a considerable degree upon Canada in many important respects.
We seem now to have marched into a new era of commonwealth interests and understanding; we have come to realize that the commonwealth is a unique and attractive political experience and we are happy to share in it as one of its senior members. There are many good reasons for this. It is important to find a bridge between the whites and the non-whites of the free world. The commonwealth serves this purpose admirably. It is important, I think, to find an English speaking counterpoise to the weight of the United States. The commonwealth does this in a loose but certainly an effective fashion. It is also important to try and discover links between those countries which are active in the free world and those countries which allege a sort of neutrality between east and west. The commonwealth provides us with this opportunity with no loss of friendship
2C8

The Address-Mr. Macnaughton or contact because of the different roads along which member states move on the highway of world order.
We are now experimenting with new opportunities for economic relationships with the commonwealth, particularly with the United Kingdom. These may or may not succeed. The conference held in Mont Trembiant last year and the proposed economic conference to be held in Montreal this September will at least give us the chance for a continuing re-appraisal of Canada and the commonwealth, and help us to see whether there are questions of an economic or political character important to Canada which should not be overlooked.
I think the success of Her Majesty the Queen's visit last year testified to the interest of Canadians in monarchy as an institution. Many hon. members will recall that the fathers of confederation at one time were considering using the term "Kingdom of Canada" but that this term was changed at the insistence of Lord Derby who feared, and I quote, that "the name would wound the sensibilities of the Yankees".
I do however, maintain that the universal acceptance by Canadians of Her Majesty the Queen as Queen of Canada is much more than an emotional outburst. We are not a new group of people isolated in a given geographical territory in North America; we are the inheritors and in fact the guardians of two great historical movements-the British and the French. To my mind the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) summarized the situation in very well chosen words when, in a newspaper article he wrote in part:
It is an inspiring thing to be a citizen of a new nation: helping to make the traditions and create the things that others will write about in a couple of hundred years. But it is a great thing also for a new country to have the roots of its nationhood buried deep in ancient freedoms and attested institutions; to inherit a long and good political tradition. As a state whose sovereign is in the line of succession from Edward the Confessor in the eleventh century we in Canada have that tradition. It emphasizes that our national story is an unbroken record, from the Magna Carta of 1215, to the assembling of parliament in Ottawa. . . . All this makes for stability and ordered progress, and it does, I think, give Canada a distinctive position in this hemisphere.
You know, the phrase "Queen of Canada" was an artificially simulated phrase a generation ago, but today men of judgment use it in its due sense and its right place in the Canadian scheme of things.
So I say that Canada is fortunate in having a unique international position. While geography would seem to confine us to the North American continent, we are in fact and in spirit members of different groups and associations. In the first place we do belong

to the North American continent with all its active contacts with our great neighbour to the south. Sharing as we do a common continent with fundamentally similar cultures, our relations with the United States must always have a special quality of immediacy in political and economic matters simply because our great neighbour is leader of the free world on the one hand and a decisive partner in the management of the affairs of North America on the other. And yet nothing is more salutary in our relations with the United States than the firmness with which we speak our piece when our interests are involved in United States policies and methods.
I do not think it is any secret that Canada's voice is listened to in Washington and exerts a certain amount of influence there. For ourselves and for our American friends this firmness is an important moderating influence in the day to day development of United States foreign policy wherever it touches upon our common problems. In the second place, Canada as a partner in NATO is closely connected with a large and very important group of western European nations. In the third place, Canada is a senior and respected member of the commonwealth family of nations and we have earned our place at the table. During the present century we have fought in three wars with our sister nations and we have co-operated with them in the endeavour to maintain and promote peace.
So I say that the commonwealth-the newest worldwide grouping of independent states alone in the world today-bridges the gulf between the old empires of the west and the new nationalisms of the Afro-Asian peoples. It unites in a community of effort the white peoples and those, whom for the want of a better term, we call non-whites. In the commonwealth we have Indians and Pakistani; we have Australians and Canadians; we have Britons and the citizens of Ghana. These and other races and faiths find an instrument for maintaining collective contact on a scale not always possible solely by bilateral associations. In this multi-national family there exists for the first time since Roman days the unifying principle of political association which transcends races, creeds and colours. For the commonwealth is in itself an entity; not a legal entity but something much more important than that; the commonwealth is a social and political idea and underlying it may be a moral notion expressed by the morality of its public law, by notions of justice, fair play and by agreement on a minimum standard of decent behaviour by those who hold power.

Thus we find that Canada although geographically a member of the North American, group of nations, also belongs through NATO to the western European group of nations and, through her commonwealth membership, to a group of ten independent states of whom four are Asian and one native African. I think it follows therefore that Canada occupies a responsible place on today's international stage. We have no domestic problems arising from colour and creed. We have, however, great experience in the art of compromise and we should be in a position to help other nations as a result of our past experience.
In short, we are ideally situated to undertake the heavy but rewarding goal of peacemaker and our achievements in this regard are already quite impressive. Certainly I think all members will agree that the recent award of the Nobel peace prize to the Leader of the Official Opposition is proof of our country's contribution to world peace and that it has been no small thing.
An outstanding example of our success in this regard was associated with the sad situation which developed in the Suez area some 18 months ago. Hon. members will recall that a deadlock developed between the United Kingdom, France and Israel on the one side and the United States on the other. I am sure hon. members will also recall that the then secretary of state for external affairs offered a formula to break the deadlock. The first part of that formula was that a United Nations emergency force should be sent to the area to end the fighting. This was done and a measure of peace restored.
The infiltration from the Gaza strip into Israel has practically ceased and that is one practical benefit besides the assurance of more or less freedom of shipping for the state of Israel.
These are practical results from the action taken, but there was a second part to that formula which involved an over-all solution of the major problems particularly concerned in the Suez area. This was supported in principle by all powers directly concerned but, so far as I am aware, there has yet been no conference to search for an over-all solution and if we ever get to a summit conference, about which we hear so much these days, I do hope and trust that the whole Middle East problem will be placed high on the agenda of such conference.
I would like at this time to digress in a manner of speaking-but only in a manner of speaking-to say that as a Canadian I am extremely proud of my country's world mindedness and I feel that in our day, when
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton the need to buttress democracy everywhere is great, we ought to pay tribute to a young nation which is democracy's leading outpost in the Middle East. I refer to Israel which is even now entering upon its second decade. We know from our own experience that the first decade in every new land is one of great historic moment; it is the period during which foundations for the future are laid; it is the time for the establishing of its place in the concert of nations and it is the time when the day to day tasks of building a country are most demanding. For our part, having had a great deal to do with the founding of the state of Israel we are morally obligated to support the new state, along with the other nations in the United Nations who agreed to its establishment.
Members of this house will recall that this year Israel is celebrating its tenth anniversary. The land of Israel is a small postage-stamp-like country of only 8,000 square miles in area and has been described as a "laboratory for human relations" and an "adventure of the human spirit". For in Israel we see the memory of ancient greatness merging with aspirations for the future and the influences of religious tradition mingling with the most advanced social and cultural thought. It is astounding what this dynamic and idealistic people have done during their first 10 years of statehood. Consider the problem we would face in this country if Canada's population had doubled in 10 years. That is exactly what has taken place in Israel. Over one million immigrants, or refugees if you wish, have gone to the new state from 79 different countries throughout the world. Consider the tightening of belts, the austerity, the sacrifice involved in settling these people, the co-operation and understanding needed in bringing about a welding of cultural streams.
Fortunately, though hailing from a diversity of countries and peoples of many tongues, they do possess in common a past history going back to bible days, an optimistic belief in the future which enabled them to reach this day, and a common sacred tongue, Hebrew, which is fast becoming secularized. Hon. members will recall that throughout the centuries, since the destruction of the original Jewish state, Hebrew had been used only for purposes of prayer and study. Now it is brought into the home, the street, the market place and into diplomatic usage. Finally, I reiterate that though coming from the four corners of the earth and from every land and clime, the Jewish people cherish in common a set of ideals, of religious beliefs and a

It has been my good fortune to have visited Israel fairly recently, and when I think of the new campus of the Hebrew university now in operation in the city of Jerusalem, greatly expanded in student body and in faculty, it is easy to see it becoming a cultural beacon of the Middle East.

a place where so many great men of past generations have made speeches.

Mr. Speaker, how could we help but point out today the great gap felt as a result of the departure of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent from Canadian politics? How could one fail to take advantage of this great opportunity to tell this house the admiration the great majority of the electors of my constituency, as well as the electors of all Canada, had for the former leader of the Liberal party? He will remain in our memories and in our hearts as the living example of gentlemanliness, of frankness and of loyalty.
And, of course, I want to say a word of appreciation and loyalty to the one who succeeded the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent at the head of the party, the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, who deserves much from the whole world for his work in favour of peace. By his last election campaign throughout Canada, in spite of the Conservative tide which literally swept the country, he earned the admiration and esteem of the majority of his fellow-citizens, no matter what their political views. His dignified way of discussing public affairs, his sense of truth and his infectious good humour, as well as his greatness in defeat, have been for all his supporters a new reason to appreciate him.
The last election campaign in my constituency of Beauce was a source of wonderment to me. By visiting each of the parishes of my constituency, undoubtedly one of the

finest of this country, I realized how deeply my electors are attached to our democratic institutions. I was able to put my finger on the most acute problems which beset them at times, and I had the opportunity to admire their courage in the face of hardship, their sense of duty and their attachment to their land, their institutions and their traditions. This electoral campaign, in a word, has caused me to love my Beauce county a little more because I have come to know it better.
La Beauce, indeed, is a riding the name of which is quite familiar to all the hon. members who sit in this house. It is the heart of an area generally known as the maple area. Surrounded by Dorchester, Frontenac and Lotbiniere ridings, it has a population of about 60,000. Its main sources of income are agriculture, industry and lumbering.
It is quite obvious to you, Mr. Speaker, that in a maiden speech and because of the short time I have at my disposal, I will not attempt to deal thoroughly with all the problems with which my constituents are faced at this time. I will in any event have the opportunity, I hope, to return to more specific subjects when we will be dealing with the estimates for the various departments. I will be content now to express the aspirations and the requests of people who, while claiming no specially favourable treatment, believe they are entitled to their just share of the benefits accruing from the laws of this country.
In the agricultural field, the situation in my constituency is such as to reflect the economic depression which extends at this time over the whole of this country. I was going to say that the situation in my constituency was possibly worse than elsewhere, in so far as one of the related industries, that is the maple syrup industry, did not receive from the government all the attention it deserved. At the last session, on the occasion of his maiden speech in this house and, subsequently, on the debate on the support price legislation, the former member for Dorchester in this house had asked the government, and more particularly the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to bring maple syrup under the terms of the new legislation. My constituents and more particularly the maple sugar producers were bitterly disappointed to note that neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the government had seen fit to listen to these recommendations. True, during the last election campaign in my constituency, the
The Address-Mr. Racine official candidate of the party in power stated on several occasions that maple sugar and maple syrup had been explicitly mentioned in the new legislation. I realize that at the time his chief concern was to obtain more votes and kinder feelings for the party in power. But now that the elections are over and that we are concerned with the interests of our people, may I be allowed to reiterate to the Minister of Agriculture the request that maple products be explicitly mentioned in the new legislation and that a support price of 30 cents per pound be provided as soon as possible so that our farmers may market their 1958 production at a reasonable price.
May I be allowed also to repeat for myself another suggestion already made in this house during the last session and to ask the government to make a substantial amount available to the maple syrup industry so that an efficient and methodical sales campaign may be carried out. In this way this tasty product will be known from one end of the country to the other and a market will be permanently established for a product whose excellence is beyond question.
A few years ago the maple sugar producers enjoyed a 33J per cent subsidy from the federal government for the purchase of aluminum buckets. The provincial government of Quebec also paid a third of the cost of these buckets, the producer paying the difference. I was very sorry to see that the government saw fit to abandon this practice which was of great advantage for our producers and I would urge the Minister of Agriculture to make this grant available once more to our sugar producers.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on the lumbering industry which is one of the most important in my constituency. We were all pleased to hear of the report of the investigation into the pulpwood combine. If I am not mistaken, this investigation was opened in 1955 at the request of several Liberal members. The report now reveals that those members were right in requesting such an investigation and we realize today that the farmers and settlers had reason to complain. It is now up to the federal government to take the necessary steps to put an end to these abuses and we hope that those steps will have the effect expected of them by our farmers and settlers who, alas, are too often the victims of exploitation by the paper companies of our province.
The woodcutting industry provides work to thousands of people in my constituency. However, because of the geographic situation

The Address-Mr. Racine of the constituency of Beauce and its proximity with the state of Maine, it so happens that the great majority of bush workers have to go to the United States to earn their living. And this leads me to speak of a subject close to my heart. I refer to unemployment insurance for our Beauce workers who are denied unemployment insurance because they work beyond our border. Other hon. members representing constituencies neighbouring on the constituency of Beauce have often explained to the house the point of view of the bush workers working on the American side of the border and deplored the fact that those Canadian citizens, who are taxpayers like all others and spend their money in Canada, are denied the advantages of unemployment insurance because of the lack of an agreement between the Canadian government and some American states.
I have made a little investigation of my own regarding some American employers and I have reason to believe that with a little cooperation on the part of the Department of Labour and of American employers, as well as on the part of local unemployment insurance offices, it would be possible to be fair to this class of my fellow-citizens who are made to suffer at this time by this lack of understanding between the Canadian government and the states concerned. The suggestions which I want to put on record are not my own, having been made before to the head office of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, but they were not acted upon for reasons which I cannot understand.
Here are the suggestions I should like to make concerning all bushworkers, teamsters, etc., in short concerning all Canadians working in the lumber industry in the states of Maine and New Hampshire and who are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits because there is no agreement with those two American states:
1-	That the company or contractor importing Canadian labour withhold 2 per cent of the gross weekly salary and turn it over to a central office in each of the states concerned. The amount thus held back should appear on a voucher, a draft of which I shall give later.
2-	This form should be completed immediately either after dismissal, voluntary departure from work or the suspension of forestry operations.
3-	Since most employees earn more than $50 a week-none of them would stay on the

job unless his net earnings amounted to that-this would make an average tax of $4 a month. The American camp is normally active nine months a year, which would make a tax of $36 a year. (That tax would run concurrently with unemployment stamps paid in Canada).
4-	To qualify for unemployment benefits, employees should be governed by the same law as is in force in Canada now, that is being unemployed and available for work, and having contributed to the funds referred to.
5-	Thousands of dollars are earned each year by Canadian lumberjacks in forestry operations in the United States, and an average of 90 per cent of that money is spent in Canada. Each year over 6,000 of our men go to camps in Maine, and if we count those of other districts like Megantic, Compton, Montmagny, Sherbrooke, Dorchester, and so on, it can be said that over 10,000 men could profit by that arrangement and draw benefits during the off-season. At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to put on the record a table of the benefits which could be paid, on the basis of the gross weekly income. As it would take some time to read and to explain the table, I would ask, Mr. Speaker, for permission to insert it directly in Hansard without reading it.

This document would contain the name and address of both the employee and the contractor, the Social Security number of the employee together with his gross salary, the amount of the 2 per cent tax, the number of days he has worked as well as the amount of tax and the full reason for the cessation of work or the departure of the employee concerned.
The copies distributed here in Canada would be equivalent to our present forms UIC 443 or 43H.
The speech from the throne mentioned the extension of the period fpr some benefits. The government must be congratulated on that effort. But I must tell the house that, under present circumstances, this extension of the benefit period will mean nothing for a great number of my fellow citizens who work in American lumber camps since they did not get the necessary stamps to be entitled to benefit from this new amendment to the act. I would therefore ask the house to take into special consideration the situation of the bush workers of many constituencies of eastern Quebec, particularly the counties of Beauce, Montmagny, l'lslet, Compton, Frontenac, Megantic etc.
A question which has been much to the fore in newspapers for almost a year is the problem of unemployment. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, much has been written in Canada with a view to establishing the responsibility of the Liberal or Conservative party in this field. Far be it from me to assess these responsibilities. The only thing I am interested in at this time is the material comfort and the welfare of the people in my riding, that is of those who are ultimately responsible for the honour conferred upon me by making me the representative of the county of Beauce.
In our part of the country, like elsewhere, unemployment has done and is still doing a lot of harm. The fact is not to be denied and my first steps in public life led me to see for myself at close quarters all the hardship caused by unemployment in my riding.
During the last federal election, the Conservative party advocated means to alleviate unemployment and stop the slowing down of
218	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Racine our economy. I am not an expert in the matter, and would not like to pose as such, but the fact remains that, in my riding of Beauce, unemployment has reached such proportions that some action, whatever it be, is urgently called for.
There has been much talk about public works; I am all in favour of that, not in ten years hence but as soon as possible. In the town of St. Georges, for instance, plans and designs are ready for the construction of a federal building capable of accommodating the post office, the R.C.M.P., the unemployment commission and other services.
What are we waiting for to undertake such works and give some employment to those unemployed heads of families of my constituency who are wondering anxiously what tomorrow will bring?
I therefore beg the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to consider this problem at once and fulfil the solemn promises made to the voters of my constituency during the last federal election. Several municipalities and towns of my constituency, such as Ste. Marie, St. Joseph, Valley Junction and others, could well benefit from a public building and would be in great need of it. Why not have those municipalities and towns benefit from the advantages that the public works program could bring to my fellow citizens of Beauce?
As a perfect counter for unemployment in my constituency, there was the problem of the Chaudiere river which each year causes damages running into thousands of dollars. I know full well that I will be told that this is a matter for the Quebec government and that the federal government is in no way concerned. Nevertheless I am surprised, Mr. Speaker, to note that two governments which managed to get along so well during an election campaign, now indulge in buck passing when the time for action has come. Since the Conservative party and the Quebec Union Nationale get along so well together, I would be very happy indeed if they showed their friendship once more, and saw to it that the people of Beauceville who live on the river's edge get the assistance to which they are entitled. We would most heartily applaud any concrete action taken by the two governments in order to remedy a situation which turns into disaster and which could well bring about loss of life.
Since the federal government is looking for ways to solve an unemployment situation which has become a cause of hardship in this country, I would suggest to them to settle once and for all that matter of the Chaudiere river, and to stop hiding behind provincial autonomy in order to avoid facing up to their responsibilities.


Another measure which could be of assistance to our jobless families, specially our large families, would of course be the increase in the rates of family allowances.
It will be recalled that, at the time of the passing of this most beneficial social legislation, the cost of living index was much lower than it is at the present time. Canadians in general and the electors of my constituency in particular would greatly appreciate the raising of the benefits from this social legislation at least in the same proportions as the old age pensions were raised in the course of the last session of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to end here my first speech in this house. I will not do so however without saying one last word on the problem which I consider as important as all other problems of a material nature, such as for instance unemployment, the economy of the country, trade, etc. etc. I refer to the great problem of national unity in Canada.
I would be the last to raise racial or religious issues against anyone in this house. During the few years when I shall have the privilege of living here among the representatives of our great Canadian family, I would wish to live in complete understanding, knowing that national unity must be exemplified in the parliament of the nation. However, understanding, co-operation and harmony do not mean subservience and still less inferiority.
In our great country made up of two great races and enriched with two cultures, it is good to know that from one ocean to the other, Canadians are at home everywhere and are everywhere the members of the same great family. Who would not be proud of this opportunity to live here and share the same feelings and ideals in spite of languages, racial origins or religions which could perhaps divide us? It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that a good way to achieve national unity, which was so much advocated in the past by the Liberal party, would be to give us a truly distinctive national flag, as the emblem of our country that has now become an adult nation of which we, Canadians, are so proud.
In concluding, I am glad to thank my electors of Beauce riding who entrusted me with their confidence, and I can assure them that I will devote every effort to their interests and those of my country, Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this is a moment which I am not likely to soon forget, rising for the first time to take part in a debate in the

House of Commons. I am very proud to have the honour to represent the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My
constituency is one which I am sure is well known to the senior members of the house and perhaps, in many ways, is just as well known to the new members. My constituency has been previously represented by very able parliamentarians. Winnipeg North Centre was first established as a constituency in 1924 and the founder and first leader of the C.C.F. party the late J. S. Woodsworth, represented this constituency from 1924 to 1943. Mr. Stanley Knowles, who in the last parliament was deputy leader of the C.C.F., represented Winnipeg North Centre from 1943 until March 31 of this year.
This is the first time that Winnipeg North Centre has been represented by a Conservative member.
Leaving March 31 and the election campaign far behind, for I am sure it is still quite fresh in the minds of hon. members, I should like to take a moment to say something about my two predecessors. Apart from party policy and party ideals, speaking only of the late Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Knowles as individuals, I say in all sincerity that I consider it an honour and a privilege to follow them as the representative of Winnipeg North Centre. It is only my hope that through an accumulation of experience in this house I shall become as gifted a parliamentarian as were both those gentlemen. I am of the firm belief that, as a very wise man once said, there is a time to speak and a time not to speak. Be that as it may, I wish to say that the voice of Winnipeg North Centre will be heard in the parliament of this country as long as I am the member for this constituency and as long as there is anyone who deserves and requires a voice in this chamber.
Before continuing I should like at this time to add to the remarks of those who have spoken before my congratulations to yourself as the Speaker of the house, to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafre-niere) and to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). In all those remarks I concur most heartily. I should also like to state as a new member one of my first impressions. It has to do with the protective staff. I have never seen a security force as competent and courteous as is this force. I am not aware of how they are trained or selected but the chief has a force of which he should be very proud. I am sure all hon. members join with me in expressing our appreciation of them.
The Address-Mr. J. MacLean
Winnipeg North Centre is composed of a broad and representative cross-section of urban people of all ethnic groups and conditions. However, we have not many occasions to use the French language and I should like at this time to associate myself with the principle that we cannot do too much to create and foster unity between the great French-speaking and English-speaking sections of our population. In this regard I should like to say:
(Translation):
On behalf of my electors of the Winnipeg North Centre riding, I welcome members who represent French-speaking Canadians.
(Text):
It would have been fanciful for me in the years gone by to have even considered that I would be a member of parliament today. At that time I did not think I should have the privilege of serving under the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Our Prime Minister is respected and revered in every home in our country for his concepts of humanity, integrity and dignity. The Canadian people realize that the Prime Minister has kept their confidence in the past and will continue to keep it in the future. We have here in the house visible proof that all Canadians have faith in the Prime Minister, in the cabinet and in the government.
Again, I had not anticipated having the privilege of listening to the oratory of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) or hearing the views and policies of the house leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation. However, I have listened very closely to the various speeches made since the beginning of the session and I feel it very necessary at this time to make reference to what I have heard in relation to the debate on the speech from the throne.
The broader aspects of the speech from the throne have been quite fully and intelligently discussed by various previous speakers. It is my opinion that the speech from the throne gives us much hope for effective measures to cope with the important problems of the future. It appears to me that our government has assumed the initiative in matters vital to the well-being of Canada. Both the members of the official opposition and the C.C.F. party have stated that the speech from the throne is most inadequate because of the omissions in it. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) said, as reported at page 45 of Hansard:
The Conservative party took office after making many promises to the people of Canada. We have now had the speech from the throne indicating that a very small part of that load of promises will be implemented during this session.

The Address-Mr. J. MacLean
It does appear that my hon. friend and the members of the opposition are not aware that the speech from the throne contains the largest program of legislation ever placed before parliament at a single session. Let me read from the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, May 17, 1958, a column written by M. J. Coldwell, national leader of the C.C.F. party. He said:
The government's program outlined in the speech from the throne is a remarkable document. Never before has so stupendous a legislative outline been placed before parliament at a single session, if it is to receive the examination and consideration it deserves, parliament will be fully occupied for many months.
Again, let me read from the editorial page of the Ottawa Journal of May 13, 1958:
A time-honoured jibe at speeches from the throne is that they conceal more than they reveal. No such reproach, surely, will be directed at the speech which opened our new parliament yesterday; so chock-full is it of promised action, much of anything concealed and to come later must mean a house in session until the snows of next winter have melted into spring.
The Journal once said of Mr. Diefenbaker that among his many remarkable characteristics was an implacable determination to carry out his promises. That indeed is what is told by this speech. Everything the Prime Minister promised in the election campaign, almost everything in fact that he as much as insinuated, is there, laid out in black and white on the parliamentary line.
The editorial ends.
Parliament, it can be said truly, has its work cut out for it, and this added: Whatever we may suffer from under John Diefenbaker's leadership it is not going to be the affliction of inaction.
If there be omissions from the speech from the throne it is only because of the impossibility to include any greater outline of legislation at this session. We are acting, the government is acting in order to direct the attention of the house to those things which we believe are of the utmost necessity to Canadians everywhere.
If I may, I should like to make a few remarks on the amendment to the amendment proposed by the C.C.F. party. The amendment reads, after the preamble:
-firstly, planned economic policies to ensure an ever-rising standard of living for the people of Canada; and.
secondly, an expanding level of international trade that will be promoted by vigorous measures to develop and expand trade with all countries.
Then, may I direct the attention of the house to the objectives of the C.C.F. party, as stated in Regina in 1933, and as previously mentioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia. We see that the most important part of the amendment has to do with complete economic planning. For such a planned economic policy the C.C.F. party would institute a full employment policy in this country. Just what exactly the policies would be are not known

at this time. However, it must be agreed that there is necessary in a completely planned economy certain dictatorial decrees, and in a completely planned economy to institute full employment those decrees would have to be implemented. I say to the C.C.F. party that such a completely planned economy could never exist in Canada today. From an ideological viewpoint a completely planned economy is, of course, the only certain solution to depressions, recessions and inflation.
But leaving this high ideological plane and proceeding to a more practical point of view which I am sure you will agree is of the utmost necessity in governing a country, it is seen that this will not be practical in any respects at all. I say this because the basic, simple reason it will not work is that the personal freedom of the individual is involved. The people of Canada still wish to choose their employment. They still wish to choose their way of living and they still wish to decide the way in which they wish to live. This has always been and will continue to be my belief. However, in support of my statements I should like to read a portion of an editorial in the Union Farmer of May 1958, written by J. F. C. Wright who is a noted observer of the Canadian political scene. I am sure that many members have read this editorial but I wish to read part of it to the house for the purpose of placing it on record. The editorial speaks of the Prime Minister and Mr. Wright, continuing with a reference to him, says:
He is not going to plan for a planned economy which would be the one way that he could put all his promises and other related ones not yet made, into co-ordinated effect. This he will not do for the simple reason that it is not his temperament to do so and, furthermore, a planned economy is not what the Canadian people want. The people want the over-all results of it without the personal involvement and inconvenience. Planned economy is inevitable here as elsewhere if the human race manages to escape annihilation as a result of an all-out war with fissionable material. But you and I are not ready to face the prospect of a planned economy because it would interfere with our individual lives and the way we think we like to live them. I might say, for instance, sure I believe in planned economy for everyone else except myself and family. X know that well-planned economy is the only certain solution to booms, busts, unemployment, depression, recession and inflation.
But how many fringe farmers with uneconomic units would be willing to turn over their acreage for long-term land conservation purposes to the government in return for being rehabilitated in order to function in some other productive activity?
How many industrial workers and labour unionists want to be told that they must, because of planned economy and resultant governmental decree, be transported forthwith to another job in another area? Or would they want the right to strike outlawed and so the establishment of wage levels beyond which the wage earners may make no further demands?

Would business and professional men relish comparable regulation concerning profits, fees and conditions of work?
As for the less visible but powerful minority of corporation executives and millionaires who sit at the controls of giant industry and finance, here no comment is necessary.
There may be an interim way to bridge the gap between free enterprise of a hundred years ago and disappearance of free markets and physical frontiers, plus the cumulative government intervention of our day. This might be by government inducement and persuasion rather than by dictatorial decree requisite in a complete planned economy.
That is all I wish to say at this time, on the amendment to the amendment. I should now like to direct my attention to the two government bills which have been passed at this session, namely the bill to extend seasonal benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act and the bill to grant additional money for house building under the National Housing Act. My constituency, like most constituencies, has great needs. In order to help it to continue in the way of progress it has given a mandate to this humble member who now requests sympathetic attention on the part of the members of the cabinet in order that I may acquit myself of this heavy task which I intend to carry out to the end in the interests of my electors.
My constituency is peopled almost entirely by working people, most of whom have large families. They are seeking through their own labour to discharge their responsibilities. However honest and generous they may be, our working people must not nevertheless consider themselves as forming an inferior class. It is as honourable a class as any other class of society. Our working men are legitimately proud of what they are. The working man is entitled to the gratitude of the government. To his ability, competence and love of work we owe almost everything that the eye can see. The honest and conscientious worker, and these traits are typical of the working class in Winnipeg North Centre, is the builder of the nation and it is our duty to recognize that fact. But those who know the greatheartedness of our workers are aware that all they seek is gainful employment.
For these reasons I am very pleased that the government saw fit to bring in legislation immediately to increase the program of public works and housing so that a considerably greater number of men and women in this country will be able to find employment. The workers of Winnipeg North Centre are also gratified that the government undertook an extension of seasonal unemployment insurance benefits for, although work is more important than unemployment insurance, it is only right that Canadian workers do not
The Address-Mr. J. MacLean suffer hardships because of unemployment that occurs through no fault of their own.
I know that the government is concerned at the present time about the unemployment problem and Canadian labour. The two measures passed in the house are evidence of the government's concern. I have great confidence that the government will do everything possible to reduce unemployment and I am well aware that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is conscientiously endeavouring, on behalf of the people of Winnipeg North Centre and the Canadian people generally, to bring about a remedy for this situation.
I should like also at this time to express the approval of the people of Winnipeg North Centre of the government's desire to establish a small business section to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them. There are many problems confronting small business at this time. The small businessmen of Winnipeg North Centre welcome the government's action on this matter.
Before concluding there are three recommendations I should like to make to the government for its attention and consideration. Part of the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, and the only part that lies outside Winnipeg proper, is the village of Brooklands. This village, as is probably the case in all small rural municipalities, needs immediate direct financial assistance. Perhaps its situation is worse than that of many other municipalities in that it borders on the city of Winnipeg and has to provide comparable living conditions with those that exist in Winnipeg.
I realize that the government is also concerned about direct assistance to municipalities in Canada. However, I direct its attention to Brooklands in particular. Here it is necessary that schools, roads, sidewalks and other local improvements be provided immediately if the village is to survive and exist in its present form. These small municipalities have a serious problem today and are entitled to the same consideration that is given to the larger towns and cities. I ask the government at this time to give consideration to the distribution of at least a portion of the reserve fund for municipalities. I cannot stress too greatly how important it is that the village of Brooklands receive some direct attention on the part of the government.
The next matter I should like to refer to the government deals with the physically handicapped people of Canada. As you are well aware, Canadians who are physically handicapped are at once in a prejudiced position with regard to employment. Employers

The Address-Mr. J. MacLean are not anxious to hire these people. The usual reason given is that they are the cause of accidents. This is certainly not the case. It has been shown to the contrary that a physically handicapped person is less likely to cause accidents while employed than a person who is not handicapped. Again, if an employer does hire a physically handicapped person he usually expects to employ him at a lower wage than the rest of his employees. The reasons given by employers are inefficiency and low production. This again has been shown not to be true. A physically handicapped person's efficiency and rate of production in his proper employment are as high, if not higher, than a normal person.
To remedy the situation I would ask that the government consider on behalf of all the physically handicapped people of Canada the setting up of a separate employment department for them in every office of the national employment service across the country. I would further ask that physically handicapped people be placed in charge of such departments and further that these people placed in charge would not only attempt to place physically handicapped people in employment but would also attempt to procure employment for them by regular consultation with prospective employers.
My last point before concluding deals with the promotion of physical development programs and athletics in Canada, and also on an international basis. I draw to the attention of the house the fact that the British empire games are being held in Wales in July of this year. A team representing the Canadian nation is to participate in these games. At the moment the Canadian team is experiencing great difficulty in obtaining the necessary finances to represent Canada at these games. I bring this matter before the house at this time, not only because I feel it is imperative that this team receive adequate support but to direct the attention of this whole house to the situation that exists in Canada today with regard to supplying the facilities and training required by our youth in promoting good, clean, wholesome athletics to improve their physical and moral standards.
I like to think that I speak with some authority, having been active in all fields of sport and particularly hockey, ever since I have been able to walk. In the matter of support for athletics in Canada and the participation of Canadian teams in international competition, it has always been my belief that the federal government should undertake to support such a national and international program. I should like to point out the seriousness of this problem by taking

the liberty of referring to some remarks made by Bill Westwick, a noted sports columnist, in his column in the Ottawa Journal on May 17 of this year. Mr. Westwick begins:
Canadian Press sports editor Jack Sullivan yesterday quoted Major Jack Davies as 'completely disgusted' with the response received by the British Empire Games' Association for funds to send Canada's team to Wales in July. Since there's just six weeks left before the team leaves, there seems ample reason for concern by Montreal chairman of the BEG association over the financial plight of Canada's entry which is supposed to number 100 athletes.
It makes you wonder about our Canadian setup in amateur and international sports when the response to an empire meet is so poor that Davies uses the term 'completely disgusted'. Something very wrong here, and not likely to be corrected until some rather drastic steps are taken. They won't be drastic so far as many other countries are concerned. But the unvarnished facts are these strictly amateur sports, which should be a great benefit to the nation, can't operate in step with the rest of the world without some revision of thinking.
From time to time you hear vague remarks about Canada sometime playing host to the Olympic games. Well it could be, but if our attitude doesn't change fairly quickly most of us will have beards as long as a javelin before it ever happens.
He goes on, and here he is referring to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith):
Even the minister will hardly suggest that the programs so urgently presented in the form of a brief by the Canadian sports advisory council would not tend to help curb the declining moral standards of our youth as well as benefit them physically. At least they wouldn't contribute to them. At the same time it would be bound to help the country's position in international sports such as the Olympics, which isn't what many feel it should be . . .
We'll grant it will require some study, but many people undoubtedly would feel more satisfied if it were tackled. They'd likely feel more satisfied too if some of the money which the Canada Council intends to hand over to the C.B.C. for cultural programs were earmarked for something along this line.
He goes on to speak of culture and a track meet and says:
You looked around at these teenagers and thought of the Massey report which nowhere included athletics as being part of Canada's culture. And then the word of the British empire games committee which has to beg its way to send a team to an empire meet, and still fail to the extent that at this stage the chairman is reported to be 'completely disgusted'.
We're not disputing the wisdom of the government's attitude towards this 'growing temptation' among individuals to expect the state to take over all society's needs. But it shouldn't be surprising to find the 'sports fan' Major Davies is counting on to help defray the Empire games expenses doing a little wondering too.
I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house on this matter, but it appears to me that this is a problem that

deserves recognition by all members of the house. We have been very proud of our athletes in the past, and particularly just recently of the Whitby Dunlops who won the international ice hockey championship. They proved to the world that Canada has some of the finest athletes. However, ice hockey is one matter; track and field, other sports and physical development are still other matters. I know, speaking from experience and on behalf of sports fans and sports-minded people of the city of Winnipeg, that facilities for physical training and an all-year-round athletic program are sadly lacking in that province. It has always been my contention that given the proper influence of the spiritual, educational, social and athletic aspects of our society, the youth of Canada cannot help but make us proud of them in the future. I again urge the attention of all members of this house, and in particular the members of the government, to the immediate problem of the British empire games and to the long-range problem of the physical development of our Canadian youth.
This session promises to be an interesting one with many subjects to discuss and problems to solve. I join with all members in expressing the hope that we may promptly and efficiently discharge our responsibilities to those who elected us and that we shall always uphold the great traditions of our Canadian parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the debate on the speech from the throne affords the earliest opportunity for private members to give voice to the problems and the complaints of their constituents, I feel it is my duty to take advantage of this opportunity and bring to the attention of this house and to the government some matters which are of vital concern not only to the people of my riding but to all the people of my province, matters which are of such an urgent nature as to demand immediate attention.
Before coming to those matters may I extend to you, sir, and to the Deputy Speaker my sincere congratulations on being unanimously elected to preside over the deliberations of this chamber. I should like also, at this time, to associate myself with all those who have complimented the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply on the excellent manner in which they made their presentation.
The first matter to which I wish to refer is the action of Canadian National Telegraphs in removing the wireless telegraph sets from their offices in Newfoundland and replacing them with radiotelephones. For the benefit of new members, I should explain that wireless
The Address-Mr. Carter telegraphy is a particularly convenient means of communication in Newfoundland, especially in my own riding where there are many small, isolated settlements, many of which are located on islands far from the land which makes the use of submarine cables prohibitive. There are other communities separated by terrain which is so difficult as to make land lines impracticable and where, in any case, the lack of roads would make maintenance impossible. I should add, too, that because the mail has to be transported over water and there are some long delays between mails, sometimes ranging from one week to three weeks, the people who live in these areas, particularly the business and professional men, are far more dependent upon telegraphic communication than people who live in other parts of Canada.
This is particularly true in the case of an accident or in times of emergency. The Canadian National Telegraphs justified their action in replacing wireless telegraph sets with radio telephones on the ground that qualified Morse operators are difficult to obtain and also that the change-over will result in improved service with a lower operating cost. As far as the first argument is concerned, I believe it is fair to say that the scarcity of Morse operators in Newfoundland is due, to a large extent, to the policy which has been pursued by the Canadian National Telegraphs since confederation. Indeed, three years ago I warned that this would be the inevitable result unless Canadian National Telegraphs policy was changed. My warning is recorded at pages 95 and 96 of Hansard of January 11, 1955, but it fell on deaf ears.
Prior to confederation there was never any difficulty in securing qualified Morse operators because every operator trained members of his own family in order that they could take over in case of illness or emergency. In addition, in almost every community there is some person suffering from some physical handicap which prevents him or her from engaging in hard manual labour. In the old days these people looked to the operation of a telegraph office as something within the limits of their physical capacity and consequently one of the few means by which they might be enabled to earn a livelihood. In our isolated communities the change in status and working conditions of postmaster telegraphers, together with loss of privileges and benefits which resulted from the taking over of telegraph offices after confederation and which are described in detail in Hansard to which I have already referred, discouraged these people from looking to telegraphy as a means of livelihood. It also discouraged operators from training their sons

NORAD-Canada-U. S. Agreement and daughters in Morse telegraphy. I am convinced that the shortage of Morse operators could be very quickly and easily overcome if pre-confederation privileges and benefits were restored.
The reduction in operational costs is going to be achieved largely at the expense of the remuneration of the postmaster-telegrapher whose princely salary averages about $135 per month for his combined services to the Post Office Department and to the Canadian National Telegraphs. I have in my file letters which indicate that as a result of this changeover the reduction in salary of these people will be substantial. One telegrapher tells me that his salary will be reduced by $500 per year. Another states that his salary will drop from $133 per month to $63 per month.
During the past nine years I have complained repeatedly against the unjust treatment accorded to that group but all to no avail. I have discussed this problem in detail on several occasions and in addition to the one just quoted detailed references can be found at page 2235 of Hansard of April 20, 1951 and at page 442 of Hansard of January 23, 1956.
The matter of salary reduction primarily is one for the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) whose department rents the services of these postmaster-telegraphers to Canadian National Telegraphs. But since this is a human problem affecting the lives and the livelihoods of people who are completely helpless to influence in any way the forces by which their fate is being determined I hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself, who so often has expressed solicitude for all the helpless and downtrodden, will take a personal interest and see to it that everything will be done to ensure fair and just treatment to these people.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.
