subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the recess I was voicing the complaints of a number of my constituents arising out of the decision by the Canadian National Telegraph Company to replace Morse wireless sets by radio telephones in order to effect savings in operating costs. I pointed out that this saving was to be obtained largely at the expense of the postmaster telegraphers whose salaries would be drastically reduced as the result of the changeover.
I should make it clear that these postmaster-telegraphers have full time jobs; they are not part time people who interrupt their ordinary work to sell a postage stamp or take a telephone call. Canadian National Telegraphs require these operators to be at hand throughout the day from nine in the morning to six in the evening, in consequence of which they are, of course, precluded from engaging in any other gainful occupation. In many centres, too, the instruments are housed in a public building at some distance from the operators' places of residence and this prevents operators from doing ordinary odd jobs around the home.
These factors should be taken into consideration along with the salary reduction to which I have just referred. The savings envisaged as a result of the changeover from one type of equipment to the other will, I believe, prove to be an illusion. There cannot be any great difference in cost between a Morse wireless set and a radio telephone, but there is a tremendous difference in the standard of service provided. The chief objection to the radio telephone is the lack of privacy; messages transmitted in this manner

can be picked up by every household radio within range. Thus messages of the utmost privacy are made known to the public at large. Canadian National Telegraphs contend that this defect has been overcome by the use of speech inverters which scramble the words and make them unintelligible when picked up on household radios. However, these inverters break down, and when this happens messages are transmitted in the ordinary way. I am informed that one of these machines failed to function about a week after it had been installed, and that in this case messages were transmitted in clear for all the public to hear. This situation lasted for several weeks until the maintenance men could return and make the necessary repairs or replacement.
Even when the inverter is functioning properly there is still some lack of privacy because the phones are not installed in soundproof booths and the messages can easily be overheard by anyone standing in the lobby of the telegraph office. I am told that an absolutely soundproof booth is a very essential item, and since such booths must be supplied if the standard of privacy is to be maintained it seems that the cost of a radio telephone plus an effective soundproof booth will together amount to a great deal more than the cost of the wireless set which is to be replaced.
The great advantage of the wireless telegraph set is that it ensures absolute privacy both with respect to people who may be standing in the lobby and also regarding interception by radio. The people of Newfoundland enjoyed this standard of privacy prior to confederation and they have every right to expect it to be maintained. I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and his colleagues in the government to work out some arrangement with Canadian National Telegraphs whereby the use of these wireless sets would be restored.
A second matter which greatly concerns my constituents is the need for improved bait supply and distribution services. The present service was initiated by the Newfoundland government about 20 years ago and a great many changes have taken place since those days. Many of the largest supply depots are no longer conveniently located and thousands of dollars are lost to Newfoundland fishermen every year through lack of a proper bait supply. The whole service needs to be completely reorganized and modernized. I intend to deal with this matter in greater detail when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries come before us for consideration, but I mention it now to 57071-3-15
The Address-Mr. Carter emphasize the urgency of this question and the necessity for immediate action with regard to this problem.
Having called the attention of the government to these most pressing matters, I turn to some of the items included in the speech from the throne. Two of the proposals, namely the extension of seasonal benefits in respect of unemployment and the increased spending of public funds for housing have already been implemented as emergency measures with the greatest co-operation from this side of the house. I will refrain from making comment on the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs and a select committee on broadcasting because there will be another opportunity to do so when the resolutions concerning these committees are brought before the house. I am sure hon. members are awaiting with interest details of the national development program, the public works program and the public investment program which constitute the government's plan to relieve the unemployment situation and reverse the serious downtrend in the economy which this country is experiencing at this time.
At the present time, as far as the opposition is concerned, these proposals are names and nothing more. As we have not yet been told what these programs consist of, and since the departmental estimates recently tabled shed no light in this respect, it will not be possible to make specific comments until detailed information about them is forthcoming from the government. We all know that communications are essential to the development of our resources, and in a general way we can agree that the building of highroads and railways is necessary to the development of our northland.
However, I think it is fair to point out that the existence of railways and highways will not in any way guarantee that development will take place. There is a striking example of this in my own riding where we have a fresh fish plant which was established through the investment of United States capital and which has now been closed down for nearly two years. The Newfoundland government acquired ownership of this plant through a first mortgage and has been trying to sell it for over a year. In June of this year the plant will be put up for public auction and I urge the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs to explore the possibilities of interesting Norwegian and other Scandinavian capital in this venture. I presume there are no immediate obstacles in the matter of exchange controls which cannot be overcome.

The Address-Mr. Carter
Norway is a country which is in many ways very similar to Newfoundland; its fishing industry is well organized and forms a very important part of its economy. Norway also has companies whose personnel are highly skilled and experienced in the operation of fresh fish processing plants. I am told that in Norway the fish industry is not subsidized and that the prices paid to fishermen compare favourably with what our Newfoundland fishermen receive.
I hope the government will act immediately on my suggestion and will have its trade commissioners explore the possibilities in this respect. There is no doubt whatever about the availability of resources; all that is required is investment capital and here is an opportunity to acquire a new, modern and first-class plant for much less than the original investment. If Norwegian or other Scandinavian capital can be interested in Newfoundland fisheries I believe it would be to the benefit of all concerned. At the same time it would be a step toward the strengthening of economic ties and the development of economic co-operation between the countries of NATO.
The flow of investment capital is to a large extent determined by world market conditions and these, of course, are completely outside the control of this government. No amount of capital spent on roads and railways can bring investment capital into Canada if market conditions are not favourable. Government encouragement of investment capital consists almost entirely of the building up of the confidence of the investor through wise fiscal and trade policies. Under Liberal administration this confidence abounded to such an extent that the problem was not to induce it to come into Canada but to keep it within the limits of the available manpower and resources in order to minimize the possibility of resulting inflationary pressures.
Since the present administration took over the absence of any well-defined fiscal and trade policy has tended to diminish the confidence of the investor and to that extent the flow of investment capital has been discouraged. This in turn has aggravated the unemployment problem by making the slowdown in our economy much worse than it would otherwise have been.
Trade is vital to Canada. With our huge productive capacity Canada must trade to survive; the only alternative is unemployment and a reduced standard of living. For this reason I support the amendment proposed on Tuesday last by my leader and the arguments which he advanced at that time.

The people of my province will be very disappointed that the speech from the throne makes no mention whatever of legislation to implement the recommendations of the royal commission with respect to term 29 of the terms of union; nor did it make mention of a floor price on fish which the Prime Minister promised when electioneering in our province, although there is a specific reference to a floor price under agricultural products. When the Prime Minister spoke in this debate last Tuesday he referred to the speech from the throne in these terms as recorded at page 32 of Hansard:
In this speech we did not have His Excellency deal with generalities. We had His Excellency ask parliament to direct its attention to those things which we believe are necessary and are of immediate importance for the benefit of the people of Canada.
I can assure him that the recommendations of the royal commission with respect to term 29 are very necessary and are of immediate importance to the people of Newfoundland. We trust that the omission of any reference to that body does not mean that their report was not expected in time for action to be taken at this session.
Before concluding I would like to make some observations about the vision of Canada which has inspired our Prime Minister and about which he spoke so often and with such great passion and eloquence during the recent election campaign.

speechtext:
I make up my own speeches. Not only do those people have a vision, they are pursuing it vigorously and relentlessly.

Our vision must be global, too, and not restricted to Canada alone. No man can live unto himself alone and neither can any nation. The whole world today is our neighbour and any lesser vision than that never can be adequate. The communist vision is based on organized materialism and if we are to survive, ours must be based on something superior because the materialism of the right is no answer at all and no match at all for the militant materialism of the left. Materialism can make men slaves but it can never set men free. Our vision must be based on something higher than material prosperity and technological achievement, something more solid than individual or sectional selfishness and greed; otherwise it is likely to turn out to be a mirage.
The strength of a nation lies in the character of its people. A nation's greatness is not determined by its technological progress, its material prosperity or its standard of living, but by the idea by which she lives and the quality of her living. There can be no substitute for integrity either in public or in private life.
Canada today has a unique opportunity to evolve a new pattern of democracy based on total honesty; honesty between electors and elected, between government and governed, between parties and between nations. In two world wars millions of people, including the flower of Canadian manhood, gave their lives for a vision, a vision of a hate-free, greed-free, fear-free world; a peaceful world; a new world order based on a new type of democracy. The world today is crying out for leadership in translating that vision into reality. The challenge to us today, and particularly to young Canada, is not so much to die for our country as to live for it so as to develop a new quality of national life that will empower Canada to speak with authority to the world because she has found the answer at home.
Canada today is called upon to lead, and if she does not lead who is she going to follow?

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak in this house for the first time, on behalf of the people of Vancouver-Kingsway may I first offer my congratulations to you, sir, on your election to the high office which you now hold and also to the other officers of this house. May I suggest that if the rest of the deliberations of this house are resolved in as wise a manner as our first act we shall have no cause for regret in the future.
I should also, of course, like to add my congratulations to the many which have already extended to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) and

To those of you who are unfamiliar with the riding of Vancouver-Kingsway I may say, that it lies entirely within the bounds of the city of Vancouver. It is a labour riding but differs from some of the other labour ridings in the respect that there is no industry within the bounds of the riding itself. Consequently, our interests are perhaps more general than some of the other ridings and we are dependent upon the basic industries and the secondary industries of British Columbia as a whole for our employment. It is, of course, in that wonderful province of British Columbia where we are celebrating our centennial and while it is a wonderful place to visit at any time, may I take this opportunity to extend a most cordial welcome to all hon. members to come out and visit us during this exceptional year when so many outstanding events are taking place. Might I suggest that if there is any information or any way that I can be of help to any who would care to make that trip, please feel free to call upon me and I assure you that I shall provide any information or assistance that I can.
Now may I get back to the matters at hand. It gives me the greatest pleasure on behalf of the people of Vancouver-Kingsway to congratulate the government on the clear and specific manner in which they have set forth their proposals to deal with the problems facing Canada today. As we have already heard from many of the previous speakers, this is the most extensive and comprehensive program that has ever been laid before a single session of parliament.
We have already passed some measures. To run over them briefly, the speech from the throne deals with those things which are needed immediately and which are of an emergent nature. It deals with things such as our public works program which go on a little bit into the future and it deals with those things which go further into the future in the developing of our north and which are already under way. Then it makes provision for the future in the development of the Arctic. Speaking of the clamour we have heard from the other side of the house in regard to unemployment, may I say that if the previous administration of which they were a part had followed such far-sighted policies as are outlined in the speech from the throne which we are examining now there would not be the need to clamour about unemployment in Canada and indeed they might still be riding in a private car instead of in an upper berth.

The Address-Mr. J. F. Browne
The first measure we had before us to deal with the emergency facing us had to do with the extension of the Unemployment Insurance Act, to extend the seasonal benefits for a period of six weeks. Many members rose to speak on it, but no one was in disagreement with it although we heard many discourses on the basic principles of socialism and many other theories. Still they were all in favour of the measure which was designed and is certainly going to help many people in Canada who would otherwise have suffered hardship provided we had followed the same plans as the previous administration and left those people to shift for themselves.
The second measure, of course, is one that deals with many problems in the country today. It had to do with the making available of $350 million more under the National Housing Act for the purpose of building more houses. Certainly there is no one in this house who can deny that this is going to have a favourable effect on the unemployment situation, as well as having the advantage of enabling a great many more Canadians to be able to own their own homes. While I am not going to go into all of the figures, because many of them are already on the record, the small loans plan which was set up last year under the Conservative administration had the effect of reducing the down payments that were necessary on houses and helping to get them down to the lower income group. It also, of course, has an effect on unemployment because it will create work for those who are producing the materials which will be used in the construction of houses as well as, as has already been pointed out, the furniture and various other things that will be used in connection with them. These are two of the immediate measures which have been taken.
To get on with some of the other things, perhaps we should next have a look at public works. Public works are another item about which we have heard a great deal from the other side of the house. We are told that the government's program is not an emergency one at all and that the projects would have been undertaken even if a Liberal administration had been returned to power. If I may be permitted to do so I should like to relate a rather amusing incident that happened during the election campaign. I believe it will throw a great deal of light on the difference between the Liberal program and Conservative policy in this regard.
The incident happened at one of those meetings where all the parties were represented. The Liberal candidate had just finished addressing the people. He had suggested to them that if they would only return a Liberal administration a great national health

program would be implemented. He said that all hospital and medical bills would be paid and everything would be wonderful. A gentleman at the rear of the audience rose and said, "Was that not in the Liberal platform in 1919?" The Liberal candidate replied, "Yes, it was but we could not rush into it. We had to build the hospitals first."
I suggest to you that some of these public works may have been undertaken under a Liberal administration but only over the period of the next 20 years and not right away as proposed by the present government.
The next matter I should like to deal with has to do with the development of our north and involves the program which was so overwhelmingly endorsed by the people of Canada on March 31. Therefore to some extent whatever debating we do on the subject now in the house can only be a repetition of the election campaign at which time the people of Canada considered this very subject and endorsed the government's program in such an overwhelming manner. Therefore I think it is quite obvious to everyone present that it must be endorsed by the members of this house.
To go over some of the projects that have been put forward, there is the proposal to build a railroad to Great Slave lake, something in which I am particularly interested on behalf of the people of British Columbia.
I wish to call the attention of the government to the fact that I should like to see provision made for the railroad to commence from a point where it will connect with the Pacific Great Eastern railway of British Columbia, thus making it possible to ship the resources of the northland when they are developed directly to the coast as well as to the province of Alberta. We do not want to do Alberta out of the benefit altogether but we most certainly want to see the line linked with the railway in British Columbia because it is most important to the country as a whole that this should be done.
There is also the plan to build roads in the northland and of course this will have a major effect on the development of resources in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and increasing their population to a great extent. Looking farther into the future, we have the proposal to provide funds for research in the Arctic area with a view to opening up the mineral resources of that area.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the matters of concern to the people of the constituency of Vancouver-Kingsway are of a very general nature. Therefore it is not going to be possible to deal with each one of them at this time because I realize there

are a great many members in the house who, like myself, are here for the first time and are anxious to present the views of their constituents. But I do wish to deal to some extent with the fishing industry which is a major segment of the economy not only of British Columbia but of Canada as a whole. Many pressing problems have arisen in this regard and there are two or three things I should like to ask the government to implement on behalf of my constituency. I am sure the government will be pleased to know that, while no doubt there are a great many things that need to be done in Canada's 265 constituencies, the proposals I intend to make will not cost any money so that the government can rest easy in that regard.
For a number of years the fishing industry has been faced with the problem of foreign nationals fishing off the coast of British Columbia. The problem has been the cause of ever-increasing concern because in some years these people, in comparison with the British Columbia fishermen, have been catching over 50 per cent of the fish taken from the waters there. But the great danger that is arising now is brought about by the fact that proper conservation measures have not been taken in the waters of the Alaskan area and therefore there is very great danger that the number of United States fishermen fishing in the waters off the British Columbia coast is going to increase.
Of course, as hon. members know, at the Geneva conference on the law of the sea the Canadian government proposed the extension of sovereignty to 12 miles from the coast rather than 3 miles as at present. The people of British Columbia were very disappointed when this proposal was rejected by the conference even though a majority of the nations voting were in favour of it. I believe that 35 nations voted in favour and 30 against but a two-thirds majority was required for the proposal to pass.
However, I should like to suggest to the government that there are many other means of implementing the proposal and that perhaps we do not need to wait for official sanction because at the moment we are actually in the position of having no international law with regard to the sea. With the many lawyers in the house perhaps I as a layman am in a rather dangerous position in discussing the subject of international law, let alone any other kind of law, but I should like to refer to one declaration which has been made by the United States. President Truman, by presidential proclamation on September 28, 1945, stated that the United States government, in view of the pressing need for the conservation and protection of

I feel that the most immediate and important matter that should come to the attention of this government is that of unemployment. This has not been a problem in my particular area in recent years, particularly at this time of the year. However, even now with high unemployment rolls, one hears about further layoffs,-I heard of that last weekend when I was home-and the closing of plants for a month or two. One hears also about men with seniority of 20 years or more receiving notices of layoffs. This is almost'unprecedented in my part of the country at this particular time. It is

true that there has been a pickup in the employment of seasonal workers, but even here the pickup has been less than expected and less than has occurred in former years. The point is that we have a large number of permanent workers idle for periods of up to one year, and few of them have the vision of a job, let alone the vision of a greater Canada that is yet to be.
I know of nothing that breaks the morale of men more quickly than does idleness and the lack of a sense of security that steady employment provides. Many of these people are doubling up in their homes, while others are losing their homes because they cannot keep up their monthly payments. In the days of security of employment many of these people bought cars, television sets and other electrical appliances so necessary in a modern home, on a monthly basis. Seizures of these articles are being made in my part of the country today and equities are being forfeited. Every job has many applicants and I cannot recall similar conditions in some of our industrial areas except in the thirties.
We would have breadlines and soup kitchens today, just as we had in the thirties, except for one thing. The former Liberal government instituted unemployment insurance benefits. We know that this fund is now being rapidly depleted. It is difficult to obtain a true picture of the unemployment situation in Canada. The last figures I saw, as of March 15, showed that the number out of work and looking for jobs stood at 590,000, up some 38,000 over the number in February. I am aware that seasonal jobs may have taken up a number, but there have been recent lay-offs and I am sure that the number of unemployed must still be very high. I saw one report which indicated that our percentage of unemployed was greater than that of the United States or that of most other countries of the western world. I read this in the New York Times, and I think the report in the New York Times said that Peru, Bolivia and Venezuela had greater unemployment than Canada.
The Conservative government will soon have been in office for a year. The unemployment in my area at least rivals that of the hungry thirties and, so far as I am aware, the government has done nothing and started nothing in the Niagara district to put one man to work. Perhaps this is a misstatement and I owe an apology to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), because he did put quite a large number of men to work on the Welland canal during the election campaign. I see the minister is not here tonight. I thought, as an employer, he treated his employees very well indeed. As an example, I saw 16 men removing snow and ice from one

of the bridges crossing the Welland ship canal. One man had a pick and was breaking up the snow and ice. The other 15 men had two shovels between them to toss it into the canal. This heyday for the local labour has now ended. Those whose loyalty was held to be the least in question were soon living either on unemployment insurance benefits or the best way they could. They did not all swallow the bait or probably I would not be here now.
The minister seems to be a kindly sort of man, and I regret that he seemed to become less solicitous for the unemployed after March 31 than he was before. May I also, Mr. Speaker, extend to you congratulations on your election to the post to which you have brought such great gifts and which you have held and hold with such great distinction. May I also offer congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. If they in their case felt any trepidation, as I certainly now feel, how much greater was their reason. Yet they showed no sign of it and they acquitted themselves in a manner that impressed us all.
With your indulgence and I suppose that of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to embark upon a brief geographical description of the riding that I represent. It is perhaps justified by the fact that the riding is a relatively new one, having been formed about half a dozen years ago from the southeast portion of Kamloops riding and the northern section of the old Yale riding, and is now called Okanagan-Revelstoke. I feel that there may be greater justification for a geographical description on an even wider scale, for on my arrival at the capital two weeks ago I had occasion to cash a traveller's cheque. I took it to a bank in the city. On entering the building I went to the first wicket at which I felt they might have any interest whatever in the modest financial transaction I wished to effect. The young lady looked at my traveller's cheque and said, "Oh, British Columbia; take it to that wicket over there". I did, and my traveller's cheque


was promptly and courteously cashed. As I stepped away from the wicket I looked up, and there was a sign overhead which said: "Foreign Exchange". I prefer not to believe that this is confirmation of a suspicion sometimes held by those of us who live west of the Rockies.
The riding I represent encompasses in its southern half the wide valleys and the rolling hills of the north Okanagan region. Moving northward it skirts the eastern section of the Shuswap lake district, then east into the Selkirk range of the Rocky mountains. It is a country of great diversity of topographical detail and there is a great diversity of interest among its people. Between those resident in the southern parts and those who reside in the most eastern section there is no great community of interest so far as the ways in which they earn their living are concerned. Activity in the southern area is largely agricultural since the region embraces sections of the fruit industry of the Okanagan valley, the dairy industry, a certain amount of beef cattle raising on the high ranges, and then beyond, and in the hills, lumber. In that section also are the rich vegetable growing areas-tomatoes and other field crops.
In this particular section of the riding there has, during the last five years, been an evident decline in the income of the people and an evident decline in the acreage under cultivation. The industry has not enjoyed the level of prosperity which it once knew and there are specific and obvious reasons why this should be the case. In the vegetable industry, with respect to tomatoes, asparagus and other specific crops; in the tree fruit industry, particularly with respect to soft fruits, the growers of that region have been subject to competition which is not, we feel, fair competition, competition which has come from south of the border and in particular from the state of California. Importations into the region have entered the Canadian market at prices which make it impossible for our industry to compete.
There are many reasons for this. The California vegetable and fruit growers have a far earlier season; their crops come into production and are harvested weeks ahead of ours and during that early period they have access to top prices and secure for the majority of their crop an income entirely adequate to their requirements. But when they are cleaning off their product and selling it at what we regard as distress prices our own crop is only just coming into the market. However, those distress prices have tended to establish the price levels at which we sell in the Okanagan region. Those prices

bear no relationship whatever to our cost of production, and consequently our industry has suffered, with the result that in many phases of our operations acreage has shrunk and hardship has been experienced.
We feel that the industry both in tree fruit and in vegetables, so far as fresh products are concerned, is entitled to a measure of protection, and it has been a cause of considerable satisfaction to many branches of agriculture in this region that the government has taken cognizance of the situation as it exists. The Agricultural Prices Support Act has already provided a measure of assistance and, in addition, the government has received delegations from the industry in recent weeks and given a sympathetic hearing to further representations from the industry. We in that region feel that subsidization is not the ultimate answer, and that it will not provide ultimate solution to our problem, but we believe our growers are entitled to equal opportunity to compete on equal terms in their own market.
The vegetable and soft fruit production of the region is not adequate to meet the total demand of the Canadian market, and thus there will always be a requirement for some importation, but it is also true, we feel, that cur commodity should have first access to the Canadian market at prices which are related to our cost of production. That is what we have sought and what the Canadian horticultural council still seeks, namely the adoption of the principle of minimum fair market value, value for duty as it is perhaps better known.
I realize, as perhaps we all do, that the implementation of such value for duty is not necessarily an easy thing owing to the obligation we have under tariff and trade agreements entered into with the United States in former years. The general agreement on tariffs and trade does not permit the indiscriminate application of value for duty, but we do feel there is an opportunity and a need for the application of this principle in meeting the problems of the tree fruit and vegetable industries of the Okanagan region. In this respect we feel that there is no cause among the Americans for retaliatory measures, because the industries do not ask either for an embargo or for increased tariff, but only for protection during that period when the Canadian products are being marketed. Once the Canadian product is marketed, then the Canadian market would be open without restriction to the fresh products of other producers. I realize that the same principle cannot apply in the case of processed products, but in the case of fresh fruit and vegetables we feel it might be applied without 57071-3-16
The Address-Mr. S. Fleming any justification for retaliation on the part of United States suppliers.
This is one of the chief problems of the region and, of course, it is a problem which has not been ignored; we know it has been the concern both of the government and of the leaders of the industry itself. Solutions are being sought, but until more adequate solutions are found than exist at present there will continue to be a degree of hardship in my riding.
The second major industry, which is located not only in the southern half of the riding but also in the northeastern section, is the lumber industry and the forest products industry generally. Much of the production from this region of the riding has gone into the export market, particularly into the United States market, and we realize that until such time as the United States economy is able to absorb Canadian lumber to the extent it was doing some time ago there is not too much that can be done by the Canadian government to restore that market. We do, however, appreciate the benefit which has accrued from the housing policies of the government and I know, also, there will be appreciation throughout the lumber industry in my riding of the benefits that will result from the measures endorsed by this house last week.
Our industry looks forward with some anticipation to the trade and economic conference which is being held in Montreal later this year because it is realized that the greatest hope for security in the industry is the expansion of our world markets, particularly for the products of our forests. We realize that the government is aware of the situation and we do appreciate what is being undertaken but there is at this moment a continuing need for every effort possible to be made to find outlets for the production of this interior region.
Within the boundaries of the riding, that is to say the northeast section I have mentioned in the Selkirk range, there are two national parks, one completely located within the boundaries of the riding and the second located in part within the boundaries. Furthermore through the Rogers pass in this region will pass the trans-Canada highway, I trust in the final stages of its completion. We can expect in a matter of a relatively short time that the highway will be completed through the mountains and that new regions which have not been readily accessible to our tourist traffic will become open to a much greater extent than ever before. This is particularly true of the two regions now classified as national parks. Mount Revelstoke national park has a mountain with a summit

The Address-Mr. S. Fleming of somewhat higher than 6,000 feet and this park has been developed to a considerable extent and is visited by great numbers of people and has been so visited for many years. However, the volume of traffic likely to enter the park and visit the mountain in the foreseeable and imminent future will be greater than its present facilities can accommodate.
Glacier national park, one of the oldest national parks in Canada, lies between Revel-stoke and Golden and is very often, I am afraid, confused with the Glacier national park in the United States. That confusion is at least true in respect to people in the western parts of our country. It is at present a wilderness park to a large extent, visited by many members of the Canadian Alpine club and other mountaineering groups but accessible only by rail and not as well known as its attractions would undoubtedly merit if it were more readily accessible. There are within that park mountains of 7,000 and 8,000 feet and higher and also the Nakimu caves which are an attraction from which the public will not be easily kept away once access to the park is made easier. At the present time, however, they are in no condition for public use, in fact they are dangerous.
In other words there is a need for consideration of the very extensive development of these two national parks during the next three years because when traffic reaches them in the numbers in Which it will reach them, accommodation must be provided to take care of the requirements and at the present time while accommodation is adequate for the time being, it needs to be expanded considerably.
This northeast region of the riding is bisected by the Columbia river. There is a very great consciousness throughout the interior of British Columbia and particularly in the Okanagan-Revelstoke region and the surrounding ridings of the latent possibilities in the development of the resources of that river. We realize there are many complexities in the negotiations which must be completed before such development can take place but we do urge the government to give every consideration to expediting those negotiations so far as it is able to do so.
We know that the future development of secondary industry throughout the southern interior of British Columbia will depend to some considerable extent upon the power resources of the Columbia. Until those resources are fully realized the potential of the region which we inhabit cannot be fully explored and that is why it is of such great significance to us.
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke).1
I am aware that the government has, during the months it has been in office, given this matter serious consideration. I can only urge on the government that this interest be maintained.
If I may now turn to a more general question-something which is not at all peculiar to the riding I represent-I would like to state that I am particularly interested in the confirmation contained in the speech from the throne that there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. As one whose business life has been associated with small business during the years in which I have been earning my own living and the majority of whose friends are engaged in small business of one kind or another, I believe this piece of legislation alone will answer a requirement, a need, a desire of many thousands of Canadian citizens. For there cannot, I think, be anything which will reach out and ultimately affect more people and their families than the application of legislation which will give small business its true place in the future development of our nation.
The small businessman has contributed a great deal to the development of Canada as a nation but in recent years the tendency has been to admire the accomplishments of giant corporations and great merchandising empires and to overlook or even completely forget the contribution made by our small businessmen over the years. I am not one of those people who believe that the day of the small businessman is over; as a matter of fact I am completely convinced that he stands at the threshold of the greatest development in the history of small business in this country.
These, Mr. Speaker, are a few of the points which came to my mind when considering the speech from the throne. There are many other questions and many other problems which confront the people I represent but I feel in regard to the legislation now in prospect that the essential requirements and the genuine needs of all Canadians-not just those in my own riding but in every riding across the country-will be well served during the life of this parliament.

I am happy to have pleased some hon. members on the treasury benches. That will not often be the case.
One of the most important matters the Conservative party has tried to minimize in this parliament and during the election was this well-known unemployment issue. Say what you will-sing it if you wish in any key-the fact remains as an hon. member stated this afternoon-that we have a winter depression and seasonal unemployment every year-but it is not each time that we have unemployment as acute as last year, and as there is even today.
I shall not look for examples in the other ridings of the province; I shall simply examine the situation in mine. As a rule in May work begins to pick up. Usually, around November and December pulp and paper companies lay off a certain number of men that they take on again in April and May. This year, instead of rehiring their employees, the Canadian International Paper laid off, only a few weeks ago, some 255 employees who had worked most of the winter, thus adding to the number of those already laid off in November and December.
It can be said therefore that the unemployment crisis is a very delicate one to settle, since being threatened by an economic crisis we are at the same time facing a danger of inflation.
I would not say that the matter is exceedingly easy for the government to solve, but

I say that, however difficult it might be, the government must make a serious effort to remedy the situation.
First I believe that a major part of our unemployment has been caused by the well known statement of the right hon. Prime Minister who said: "We are going to take 15 per cent of our present trade with the United States and divert it to the United Kingdom." This was, I feel, an utterly childish statement, coming from a statesman. If he had thought five minutes before uttering those words, he would have never said them, and I know that he is already sorry for his statement. I know that even if the United States have made no official representations to Canada following that change of policy, some people have been alarmed unofficially and only a few weeks after that statement, we already felt the consequences of trade difficulties existing between Canada and the United States.
In the paper industry particularly, paper is being bought, for instance, from Scandinavian manufacturers. Owing to the low salaries paid in those countries, paper can be produced at a lower price and the United States can buy it at about the same price as Canadian made paper, although shipping costs are higher.
By thus eliminating part of the American paper purchases in Canada, not only the paper industry but also the forest industry are affected. Thousands of our people are earning their living in the forest industry and thousands of our farmers, during the winter months, try to supplement their revenue by working in the forest.
This state of affairs is due to a great extent to that unwise and blundering statement and I contend that we must now try the impossible to correct that situation. In spite of the statements made, I still believe that we have yet in the United States a very important market which we can recover. To achieve that purpose, however, the present cabinet ministers will have to travel and become salesmen. Oh! it is a wonderful thing to become a cabinet minister, but if one does not travel, one does not find the necessary markets. Salesmen, at this time, have to go from door to door to sell their goods. So our ministers should have to go from country to country because we need new markets. If we do not find some, the present unemployment situation will continue and will become intolerable.
The people are dissatisfied, they are stirred up. Something must be done. Some may say that there is danger of inflation. That is possibly true. Is that why the government did not mention any tax reductions such as had been proposed by the chief of the

Liberal party? I believe that it is not necessarily through public works that the unemployment situation can be solved. Of course I am all for public works but we all know that before they can be carried out, preparations have to be made, reports have to be obtained from engineers, plans have to be studied, in short, everything has to be organized and that takes many months. There has been talk of public works since the beginning of the last election campaign but what public works have been initiated? There is talk of public works which are required in the far north, of railways for the far north. How can construction of highways in the Northwest Territories be of any assistance to the great number of unemployed people who are mainly in the eastern part of the country? We would have to transfer people and take them away from their families. Jobless or not, these people have feelings and they prefer staying among their own people. Some way has to be found to help our section of the country, and the best way is the one proposed by my leader: tax reductions.
I well recall that the right hon. Prime Minister, who himself was in the midst of an election campaign, tried to ridicule the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Well, I see in a New York newspaper that Mr. Harriman ...

Well, I share the opinion of those American experts who are also feeling the effects of a certain depression, perhaps lesser than ours, in view of their enormous population. But, to my mind, we should first lower taxes and then carry out public works.
I am indeed happy to note that the speech from the throne refers to all kinds of public works. And then here:

Since the present government is of the opinion that public works must be undertaken to alleviate the unemployment problem, I would ask it not to forget this particular project which is needed in the Hull-Ottawa area, the interprovincial bridge.

America Act, the central government has access to all fields of taxation in our country. Well, since the central government is in the best position to collect the money necessary for its purposes and since, if need be-as is recognized by economists-it may resort to deficit budgeting in periods of recession, I urge the central government to open its purse and help municipalities and provinces to undertake public works of their own.
I note there is also mention of television. This subject of television has given rise to all sorts of comments throughout the country. I must say, to the credit of state television, that it has made giant strides.
The C.B.C. offers well-balanced programs that are often better than anything coming from the United States. I am proud to give the corporation due credit. It is utterly impossible. No head of a family would want to take such a risk.
Well, the federal government which has means at its disposal, must find the money it needs to help those people to keep on studying so that Canadians may benefit from values which are here in a dormant state and ready to be developed. I had in mind Mr. Speaker, to deal with the parliamentary system itself, but I believe that I will not have the time to do so. I am only going to make a brief reference to it.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION AND OPERATION OF THE NORTH AMERICAN AIR DEFENCE COMMAND CANADIAN EMBASSY WASHINGTON, D.C. No. 263

speechtext:
May 12, 1958.
Sir,
I have the honour to refer to discussions which have taken place between the Canadian and the United States authorities concerning the necessity for integration of operational control of Canadian and United States air defences and, in particular, to the study and recommendations of the Canada-United States military study group. These studies led to the joint announcement of August 1, 1957, by the Minister of National Defence of Canada and the Secretary of Defence of the United States, indicating that our two governments had agreed to the setting up of a system of integrated operational control for the air defences in the continental United States, Canada and Alaska under an integrated command responsible to the chiefs of staff of both countries. Pursuant to the announcement of August 1, 1957, an integrated headquarters known as the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD) has been established on an interim basis at Colorado Springs, Colorado.
For some years prior to the establishment of NORAD, it had been recognized that the air defence of Canada and the United States must be considered as a single problem. However, arrangements which existed between Canada and the United States provided only for the co-ordination of separate Canadian and United States air defence plans, but did not provide for the authoritative control of all air defence weapons which must be employed against an attacker.
The advent of nuclear weapons, the great improvements in the means of effecting their delivery, and the requirements of the air defence control systems demand rapid decisions to keep pace with the speed and tempo of technological developments. To counter the threat and to achieve maximum effectiveness of the air defence system, defensive operations must commence as early as possible and enemy forces must be kept constantly engaged. Arrangements for the co-ordination of national plans requiring consultation between national commanders before implementation had become inadequate in the face of a possible sudden attack, with little or no warning. It was essential, therefore, to have in existence in peacetime an
organization, including the weapons, facilities and command structure which could operate at the outset of hostilities in accordance with a single air defence plan approved in advance by national authorities.
Studies made by representatives of our two governments led to the conclusion that the problem of the air defence of our two countries could best be met by delegating to an integrated headquarters, the task of exercising operational control over combat units of the national forces made available for the air defence of the two countries. Furthermore, the principle of an integrated headquarters exercising operational control over assigned forces has been well established in various parts of the North Atlantic treaty area. The Canada-United States region is an integral part of the NATO area. In support of the strategic objectives established in NATO for the Canada-United States region and in accordance with the provisions of the North Atlantic treaty, our two governments have, by establishing the North American Air Defence Command recognized the desirability of integrating headquarters exercising operational control over assigned air defence forces. The agreed integration is intended to assist the two governments to develop and maintain their individual and collective capacity to resist air attack on their territories in North America in mutual self-defence.
The two governments consider that the establishment of integrated air defence arrangements of the nature described increases the importance of the fullest possible consultation between the two governments on all matters affecting the joint defence of North America, and that defence co-operation between them can be worked out on a mutually satisfactory basis only if such consultation is regularly and consistently undertaken.
In view of the foregoing considerations and on the basis of the experience gained in the operation on an interim basis of the North American air defence command, my government proposes that the following principles should govern the future organization and operations of the North American air defence command.
(1)	The commander-in-chief NORAD (CIN-CNORAD) will be responsible to the chiefs of staff committee of Canada and the joint chiefs of staff of the United States, who in turn are responsible to their respective governments. He will operate within a concept of air defence approved by the appropriate

NORAD-Canada-U.S. Agreement authorities of our two governments, who will bear in mind their objectives in the defence of the Canada-United States region of the NATO area.
(2)	The North American air defence command will include such combat units and individuals as are specifically allocated to it by the two governments. The jurisdiction of the commander-in-chief, NORAD, over those units and individuals is limited to operational control as hereinafter defined.
(3)	"Operational control" is the power to direct, co-ordinate, and control the operational activities of forces assigned, attached or otherwise made available. No permanent changes of station would be made without approval of the higher national authority concerned. Temporary reinforcement from one area to another, including the crossing of the international boundary, to meet operational requirements will be within the authority of commanders having operational control. The basic command organization for the air defence forces of the two countries, including administration, discipline, internal organization and unit training, shall be exercised by national commanders responsible to their national authorities.
(4)	The appointment of CINCNORAD and his deputy must be approved by the Canadian and United States governments. They will not be from the same country, and CINCNORAD staff shall be an integrated joint staff composed of officers of both countries. During the absence of CINCNORAD, command will pass to the deputy commander.
(5)	The North Atlantic treaty organization will continue to be kept informed through the Canada-United States regional planning group of arrangements for the air defence of North America.
(6)	The plans and procedures to be followed by NORAD in wartime shall be formulated and approved in peace-time by appropriate national authorities and shall be capable of rapid implementation in an emergency. Any plans or procedures recommended by NORAD which bear on the responsibilities of civilian departments or agencies of the two governments shall be referred for decision by the appropriate military authorities to those agencies and departments and may be the subject of inter-governmental co-ordination.
(7)	Terms of reference for CINCNORAD and his deputy will be consistent with the foregoing principles. Changes in these terms of reference may be made by agreement between the Canadian chiefs of staff committee and the United States joint chiefs of staff, with approval of higher authority as appropriate, provided that these changes are in consonance with the principles set out in this note.

(8)	The question of the financing of expenditures connected with the operation of the integrated headquarters of the North American Air Defence Command will be settled by mutual agreement between appropriate agencies of the two governments.
(9)	The North American Air Defence Command shall be maintained in operation for a period of ten years or such shorter period as shall be agreed by both countries in the light of their mutual defence interests, and their objectives under the terms of the North Atlantic treaty. The terms of this agreement may be reviewed upon request of either country at any time.
(10)	The agreement between parties to the North Atlantic treaty regarding the status of their forces signed in London on June 19, 1951, shall apply.
(11)	The release to the public of information by CINCNORAD on matters of interest to Canada and the United States of America will in all cases be the subject of prior consultation and agreement between appropriate agencies of the two governments.
If the United States government concurs in the principles set out above, I propose that this note and your reply should constitute an agreement between our two governments effective from the date of your reply.
Accept, sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
"N. A. ROBERTSON" Ambassador of Canada.
The Honourable John Foster Dulles,
Secretary of State of the United States, Washington, D.C.

May 12, 1958.
Excellency,
I have the honour to refer to Your Excellency's note No. 263 of May 12, 1958 proposing on behalf of the Canadian government certain principles to govern the future organization and operation of the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD).
I am pleased to inform you that my government concurs in the principles set forth in your note. My government further agrees with your proposal that your note and this reply shall constitute an agreement between the two governments, effective today.
Accept, Excellency, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
"CHRISTIAN A. HERTER" for the Secretary of State.
His Excellency Norman Robertson,
Ambassador of Canada.
